en: The Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtra. Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.

The First Book. Now, therefore, follows the ritual for the domestic *sthālīpāka* offerings. Having swept around [the site], smeared it with cow-dung, drawn lines upon it, removed the dust, sprinkled it with water, and established the fire; having spread out a seat for the *brahmán* priest to the south, carried forward the water, strewn grass around the fire, placed the necessary items in their proper places, prepared two strainers (*pavitra*), consecrated the sprinkling-water (*prokṣaṇī*), sprinkled the required items, poured out the clarified butter (*ājya*) and placed it over the fire, one should perform the circumambulation with fire (*paryagni-karaṇa*).

Having heated the *sruva* ladle, wiped it, sprinkled it with water, heated it again, and set it down; having taken out the clarified butter (*ājya*), purified it, inspected it, and prepared the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling waters as before; having taken up the *upayamana* grass-bunches, placed the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) on the fire, and sprinkled water around it, he should offer the oblation. 3–4.
This same rule applies wherever there is an oblation (homa). 5.
The establishment of the domestic fire (āvasathya) occurs at the time of marriage; according to some, it occurs at the time of inheritance. 2.
Having brought fire from the house of a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle,
everything [is performed] as in the case of the *cātuṣprāśya* cooking;
some say that the handing over of the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) is also included.
According to the Śruti, "There are five great sacrifices" (6).

Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* for the deities of the *agnyādheya* and having offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), he offers eight oblations of clarified butter with the following verses first:

"O Agni, do thou protect us," "O Agni, be thou ours," "This my prayer, O Varuṇa," "I approach thee," "Those which are thy hundred," "O Agni, [the sin] from the gods," "Upwards the highest," and "Be there for us" (7–8).

Thus, having offered the sthālīpāka above to the deities of the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), he makes an offering to Sviṣṭakṛt as well, with the verses: "O Agni Ayāsya, that which was offered with vaṣaṭ, whatever I have overstepped in the ritual—O gods, you who know the path. 9–11.
Having offered the *barhis* grass, he eats;
then follows the feeding of Brahmins.
There are six persons worthy of the *arghya* offering: the teacher, the officiating priest, the bridegroom, the king, a dear friend, and the *snātaka*.
They should honor [the guests] every year;
however, those officiating priests who are about to perform a sacrifice should be honored as follows:
having brought forth a seat, one says, "Please, sir, be seated; we shall honor you."

They bring a seat, water for the feet, water for the feet, water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka)—curds, honey, and ghee—contained in a bronze vessel, covered with another bronze [lid]. Another person announces the items, beginning with the seat, three times each.
He accepts the seat.

"I am the pre-eminent among my equals, like the sun among those that rise; I step upon this one who would seek to harm me"—with these words, he steps upon him. Another [student] sits on a seat at his feet.
Having washed the left foot, he washes the right foot.
If he is a Brāhmaṇa, [the guest] first [takes] the right [hand].
(11) "Thou art the milking of Virāj; may I obtain the milking of Virāj; for my feet, the milking of Virāj.
(12) He accepts the *arghya* water with the formula: "Ye are waters; through you may I attain all desires. (13)

While pouring [the water] away, he recites the consecration formula: "I send you forth to the ocean; go to your own source. May our heroes be unharmed; let not their vigor flow away. (14) He sips water, saying: "Having come hither, unite me with glory and splendor. Make me dear to all creatures, a lord of cattle, and bring safety to my body. (15) With the words, "Of Mitra thee," he gazes at the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). (16)
He receives it with the formula, "Thee for the god" (devasya tvā).

Having placed it in his left hand, he stirs it three times with the ring finger of his right hand, saying: "Homage to the dark-faced one, the consumer of food! That which is stuck to thee, that I cut away from thee.
He then sprinkles it three times with the ring finger and thumb.

He eats three mouthfuls [of honey], [reciting]: "Whatever is the most excellent form of honey, the essence of honey, the food—by that most excellent form of honey, the essence of honey, the food, may I become most excellent, an eater of the essence of honey, and an eater of food.
Or he may eat with verses containing the word "honey," verse by verse.
He should give the remains to his son or to a pupil seated to the north.
Or he may eat it all;
23 or he may pour it out in a place where no path is made before [the fire].

24 Having sipped water, he touches his vital organs with the formula: "Speech in my mouth, breath in my nostrils, sight in my eyes, hearing in my ears, strength in my arms, vigor in my thighs; may my limbs be uninjured, and may my body be united with my body. 25
When he has sipped water, [the teacher] takes up a blade of grass and says three times, "O Cow!

He replies: "If he should slaughter her, he says: 'She is the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, the navel of immortality. I speak for the sake of one who understands; do not slay the sinless, innocent Aditi! I strike away the evil of both myself and so-and-so. "Then, if he should wish to release her, he should say: 'The evil of both myself and so-and-so is struck away! Release her! Let her eat grass! (26–28)
But the honorarium (argha) must never be without meat;
one should simply say, "Prepare it for the sacrifice" or "Prepare it for the wedding," for according to the Śruti:
"Even if one should sacrifice with Soma more than once in a year, they should officiate for him only after the arghya has been prepared, not before."

There are four *pākayajñas*: the *huta*, the *ahuta*, the *prahuta*, and the *prāśita*. (1) These five are performed outside the hall: the wedding, the tonsure ceremony, the initiation, the cutting of the beard, and the parting of the hair. (2) Having smeared the ground, raised it, and sprinkled it with water, one should establish the fire. (3)
Some [prescribe] kindling by friction at the wedding;
on the northern course of the sun, during the waxing fortnight, on an auspicious day, he should take the hand of a maiden.
[He should do so] under three of each of the asterisms beginning with Uttarā.
Under Svāti, Mṛgaśiras, or Rohiṇī—
these three [days] are for a Brāhmaṇa according to the sequence of the social classes;
two [days] are for a Rājanya.
One [verse] for a Vaiśya (10).
Some say that for all [classes], including a Śūdra, [the rite is performed] excluding the mantras (11).

Then he causes her to put on a garment with [the verse]: "Go to old age; put on the garment; become the protector against the curse of the people. Live a hundred autumns, full of luster; clothe yourself in wealth and sons. Long-lived one, put on this garment" (12).
Then the upper garment: "The goddesses who spun [the wool], who wove it, and who stretched the threads all around—you, O goddesses, clothe yourself in this for long life;

put on this garment, O long-lived one. (13) Then he makes them both anoint each other: "May the All-gods anoint our two hearts together, may the Waters, may Mātariśvan, may the Uniter, and may the Ordainer unite us. (14)

Having taken her, who was given by her father, he goes out [from the house], saying: "Whether you have gone far in your mind, O Pavamāna, or toward the quarters, may the golden-winged Vaikarṇa make you one whose mind is intent on me—[Name]! (15)

Then he makes her look at him: "Be one whose eye is not terrible, not a slayer of her husband; be auspicious toward the cattle, well-disposed, and full of splendor. A mother of heroes, desiring the gods, be pleasant to us—be a source of welfare for our bipeds and a blessing for our quadrupeds. Soma first obtained you; the Gandharva obtained you next. Agni is your third husband; your fourth is born of men. Soma gave you to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave you to Agni. And Agni has given you to me, along with wealth and sons."
"May that Pūṣan lead us most auspiciously; may she, longing for us, part our thighs. In her we longingly insert our member; in her many desires are established.
(16) Some [teachers] say that she should go around the fire keeping it to her right.
Behind the fire, having stepped upon a broom or a mat with her right foot, she sits down. (2)

While [the disciple] maintains contact, [he performs] the two libations (āghāra), the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), the Mahāvyāhṛtis, the universal expiation (sarvaprāyaścitta), the offering to Prajāpati (prājāpatya), and the Sviṣṭakṛt.
This is the constant rule everywhere.
Before the Mahāvyāhṛtis, the Sviṣṭakṛt is performed if the sacrificial oblation (havis) is other than clarified butter.
This interval between the *prājāpatya* and the *sarvaprāyaścitta* is the place for insertion (*āvāpasthāna*) in a marriage ceremony:
(6) when one desires the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings, and when one knows the *jayas* and *abhyātānas*;
(7) because of the statement, "By whatever rite one might be deficient... (8).

Mind and mentation, intention and purpose, the known and the act of knowing, the mind and the Śakvarī verses, the new moon and the full moon, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara. Prajāpati gave the Jaya hymns to Indra the Bull, he the fierce one, for the conquest of armies. To him all the people bowed down; he became fierce and worthy of invocation here. Svāhā! 9

Agni is the lord of beings; may he protect me. Indra is the lord of the eldest; Yama of the earth; Vāyu of the intermediate space; Sūrya of the sky; Candramas of the stars; Bṛhaspati of sacred knowledge; Mitra of truths; Varuṇa of the waters; the Ocean of rivers; Food of sovereignties—may that protect me. Soma is the lord of plants; Savitṛ of instigations; Rudra of cattle; Tvaṣṭṛ of forms; Viṣṇu of mountains; the Maruts are the lords of hosts—may they protect me. Fathers and grandfathers!

"May my fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers—those who have passed away and those who are yet to come—protect me here in this sacred knowledge (*brahman*), in this sovereignty (*kṣatra*), in this blessing (*āśis*), in this priestly office (*purodhā*), in this rite (*karman*), and in this invocation of the gods (*devahūti*)—*svāhā*! He appends this formula everywhere. 10.

May Agni, the first among the gods, come; may he release her offspring from the noose of death. May King Varuṇa grant his approval for this, so that this woman may not weep over the calamity of losing a grandson—*svāhā*. May Agni Gārhapatya protect her; may he lead her offspring to a long life. May she have a living mother with an unfailing lap; may she fully experience the joy of a grandson—*svāhā*.

"O Agni, worthy of sacrifice, bestow upon us from heaven and from earth all things for our well-being. Whatever is great and praiseworthy born in this world or in heaven—that wonderful wealth, bestow it upon us, Svāhā! 'O Agni, show us a good path; point out the way and come to us. May your life be full of light and free from decay. Let death depart; immortality has come to us. May the son of Vivasvat grant us freedom from fear, Svāhā!
Some recite 'Beyond death... at the end of the consumption [of the remains]."

The bridegroom’s brother pours fried grain mixed with *śamī* leaves into her joined palms with his own joined palms. Standing with joined hands, she offers it as an oblation: "May the maiden worship the god Aryaman at the fire; may the god Aryaman release her from here, so that she does not fall from her husband—*svāhā*! This woman speaks thus, scattering the fried grain: 'May my husband be long-lived; may my kinsmen prosper—*svāhā*! I scatter these fried grains into the fire for the sake of your prosperity. May Agni grant his approval to this union of mine and yours—*svāhā*! " (2)

Then he takes her right hand, including the thumb, with the verse: "I take your hand for the sake of good fortune, so that you may reach old age with me, accompanied by offspring. Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—the gods have given you to me for the householdership. "I am he (Ama), you are she (Sā); you are she, I am he."

"I am the Sāman, you are the Ṛc; I am the sky, you are the earth. Come, let us two marry; let us deposit seed together; let us procreate offspring; let us find many sons. May they reach old age; may we two, as a loving couple, radiant and well-disposed, see a hundred autumns, live a hundred autumns, and hear for a hundred autumns.

Then he makes her step upon a stone to the north of the fire with her right foot: "Step upon this stone; like a stone, be thou firm. Tread down those who attack us; crush those who seek to fight against us."

Then he sings the verse: "O Sarasvatī, protect this [sacrifice], O blessed one, rich in prizes! You whom all beings at the beginning of this creation, in whom all that has come to be and this entire world have arisen—that song I shall sing today, which is the highest glory of women.
(2) Then they both walk around [the fire] while reciting: "For you, O Agni, they first led Sūryā away with her bridal procession; give back the wife to her husbands, together with offspring.
(3) In this same manner, the second time, the parched grain and so forth [are offered]. (4)
With the fourth [verse], he pours all the parched grains (*lāja*) from the winnowing basket with the formula: "To Bhaga, svāhā! (5).

Having offered the *prājāpatya* oblation for her who has been led around three times, (6) he then makes her step seven steps toward the north with the formulas: "One for food; two for strength; three for the increase of wealth; four for well-being; five for cattle; six for the seasons; O friend, be a seven-stepper; be devoted to me. (1)
He appends the formula "May Viṣṇu lead you" to every [verse]. 2.
Having placed a water-pot on his shoulder from the time of the departure onwards, he stands to the south of the fire, remaining silent. 3. According to some teachers, he stands to the north. 4.

Then he sprinkles her on the head with the verse: "May the waters, auspicious, most auspicious, peaceful, most peaceful, make medicine for you. (5) And with the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are best" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā*).
(6) Then he makes her look at the sun with the verse: "That eye" (*taccakṣuḥ*). (7)
Then he places his right hand upon her heart, saying: "I place your heart in my vow; let your mind follow my mind; enjoy my word with a single-minded focus; may Prajāpati join you to me.
(8) Then he addresses her with this mantra: "This bride is most auspicious; come together and behold her. Having bestowed good fortune upon her, depart for your homes. (9)

A strong man, having lifted her up, causes her to sit down on the skin of a red bull, which has been placed in a well-concealed house, either towards the east or the north, with the words: "Here let the cows sit down, here the horses, here the men; here let the sacrifice with its thousand-fold dakṣiṇā sit down, and here let Pūṣan sit down.
And they should pronounce the name of the village, because of the statement: "One should enter the village at a wedding and at a funeral."
Therefore, according to the Vedic revelation, the consensus of those two is authoritative. 13.
He gives a gift to the teacher. 14.
A cow is the gift for a Brāhmaṇa. 15.
A village for a Kṣatriya (16), a horse for a Vaiśya (17),
and a hundred cows plus a chariot for one who has daughters (18).

When the sun has set, he shows her the pole star (*dhruva*), saying: "Thou art firm; I see thee as firm. Mayst thou be firm in prosperity for me. Bṛhaspati has given thee to me. With me as thy husband, live a hundred autumns, blessed with offspring.
(19) If she should not see it, she should nevertheless say, "I see it.
(20) For three nights, they two should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, and sleep on the ground.

They should sleep together for one year, but they must not engage in sexual intercourse; [or] for twelve nights, six nights, or at least three nights. 21. From the time of taking the firewood for the *upayamana* onwards, there is the maintenance of the *aupāsana* fire. 1. With curd, rice grains, or unbroken rice, [the offering is made] during the times when the sun has either set or not yet risen. 2.
"To Agni, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā!"—thus in the evening.
"To Sūrya, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā!"—thus in the morning.
"Mitra and Varuṇa are males; both Aśvins are males; Indra and Sūrya are males."
"May a male abide in me; again, *svāhā*!"—thus [she should sacrifice] the first oblation if she desires a child.
Two draft-oxen are the sacrificial fee (3);
the expiation is [as prescribed] (4); then follows the feeding of Brahmins (5).

On the fourth night, in the latter part of the night, having kindled the fire within, having seated the Brahman priest to the south, having placed a vessel of water to the north, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (oblation of boiled rice), and having offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), he offers oblations of clarified butter.

O Agni, you are the expiation of the gods; as one seeking protection, I, a Brāhmaṇa, approach you. Destroy that body of hers which is husband-slaying; Svāhā! O Vāyu, you are the expiation of the gods; as one seeking protection, I, a Brāhmaṇa, approach you. Destroy that body of hers which is progeny-slaying; Svāhā!

O Sūrya, expiation! You are the expiation of the gods; I, a Brāhmaṇa desiring protection, approach you for refuge. Whatever body of hers is destructive to cattle, destroy that for her—Svāhā! O Candra, expiation! You are the expiation of the gods; I, a Brāhmaṇa desiring protection, approach you for refuge. Whatever body of hers is destructive to the household, destroy that for her—Svāhā! O Gandharva, expiation! You are the expiation of the gods; I, a Brāhmaṇa desiring protection, approach you for refuge. Whatever body of hers is destructive to fame, destroy that for her—Svāhā! (2)

He offers of the *sthālīpāka* with the formula, "To Prajāpati, svāhā! (3). Having offered each of these oblations, he pours the remnants into a vessel of water and then sprinkles her on the head with it, saying: "That body of yours which is husband-slaying, offspring-slaying, cattle-slaying, house-slaying, glory-slaying, censurable, and which brings about the death of paramours—that I make [thee] from this; may you, O so-and-so, grow old together with me. (4) Then he makes her eat the *sthālīpāka*, saying: "I join your breaths with my breaths, your bones with my bones, your flesh with my flesh, and your skin with my skin. (5)

Therefore, one who knows this should not seek to joke with the wife of a learned *śrotriya*, for such a person becomes even more [rigidly] observant. Having married her, he may enter her according to the season;
or he may act according to his desire, because of the scriptural statement: "Let us two unite as long as we have the power of procreation."

Then he touches her right breast with his heart: "O thou of beautiful brows, that heart of thine which rests in the sky in the moon—I know it; may it know me. May we see for a hundred autumns, may we live for a hundred autumns, may we hear for a hundred autumns.
Thus from this point onwards.

On the first day of the lunar fortnight and other such occasions, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* and offered oblations to the deities of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, he makes offerings to Brahmā, Prajāpati, the Viśvedevas, and Heaven and Earth.
(1) He performs the offering of food (*bali*) to the Viśvedevas, to the household spirits, and to Space.
(2) He offers into the fire of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice with the formulas: "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Prajāpati! Svāhā to the Viśvedevas! Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt! (3)

Outside, he offers a sacrifice of women with the mantra: "Homage to the woman! Homage to the man! Homage to the aged and the young! Homage to the white one with black teeth, the lord of sinners! Homage to those who harass my offspring, whether they dwell in the village or in the forest; let there be homage to them, I offer this oblation to them; may it be well with me, may they grant me offspring.
(4) Having washed the remains with water, he then feeds the Brāhmaṇas. (5)

If she does not conceive, one should fast on the day of the *śvetapuṣpī* (white-flowered) *siṃhī* plant, and on the constellation *Puṣya*, having extracted the root, on the fourth day when she has bathed, one grinds it with water at night and pours it into her right nostril, saying: "This is the protecting, overcoming herb, Sarasvatī; I, the son of this great one, have grasped its name as a father [grasps his son's].
This is the *puṃsavana* (rite for ensuring a male child).

In the second or third month, when the fetus first moves, on a day when the moon is in conjunction with a male asterism, he should fast, bathe the child, and dress him in two unwashed garments. Then, having ground the shoots and buds of the *nyagrodha* tree at night with water, he should pour [the mixture] over him as before, using the two verses beginning, "Hiraṇyagarbha" and "From the waters was he gathered.
Some also add a thorn of *kuśa* grass and a shoot of *soma*.
Having placed a tortoise-bile on the lap, if he should desire, "May he be vigorous," he consecrates him with the *vikṛti* mantra, "Thou art a Suparṇa," prior to the Viṣṇu-strides. 5.
Now follows the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*). 1.

As in the *puṃsavana* rite, during the first pregnancy, in the sixth or eighth month, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* mixed with sesame and mung beans, and having offered an oblation to Prajāpati, she sits on an auspicious seat (*bhadrapīṭha*) to the west of the fire. With an even number of ears of grain tied together, with three stalks of *darbha* grass, with a porcupine quill from a three-colored animal, with a shoot of the *vīratara* plant, and with a full spindle, he parts her hair upwards, saying: "Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ."
Or he ties on the triple-stranded [cord] with each of the great *vyāhṛtis* [saying]: "This tree is full of vigor; be thou full of vigor and fruit-bearing. Then he says:
"Let the lute-player and the singer sing of the king, or whoever else is more heroic."

Some also cite this verse: "Soma alone is our king; may these human subjects remain with their wheel unyoked on your bank"—here he utters the name of the river by which she has settled. (8) Then follows the feeding of Brahmins.
(9) He sprinkles her with water when she is about to give birth, [reciting] "Let him stir, the ten-month-old," and "Before whom you... (10).

Then follows the casting away [of the placenta]. "Let the speckled *śevala* go down for the dog to eat the afterbirth; let it not lie upon the flesh nor in any dwelling place; let it fall away from the afterbirth.
(2) While the umbilical cord of the newborn boy is still uncut, he performs the rites for the production of intelligence and long life.

(3) With his ring finger, covered with gold, he causes [the child] to taste honey and ghee, or ghee alone, [with the words]: "Bhūḥ! I place thee in me. Bhuvaḥ! I place thee in me. Svaḥ! I place thee in me. Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ! I place everything in thee. (4)

Then he performs the rite for longevity. He mutters [the following] at the navel or in the right ear: "Agni is long-lived; he is long-lived through the trees. By that longevity, I make you long-lived. Soma is long-lived; he is long-lived through the plants. By that longevity, I make you long-lived. The Brahman is long-lived; it is long-lived through the Brāhmaṇas. By that longevity, I make you long-lived. The gods are long-lived; they are long-lived through immortality. By that longevity, I make you long-lived."

"The seers are long-lived; they are long-lived through their vows. With that life-force, I make you long-lived. The fathers are long-lived; they are long-lived through the *svadhā* offerings. With that life-force, I make you long-lived. The sacrifice is long-lived; it is long-lived through its sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). With that life-force, I make you long-lived. The ocean is long-lived; it is long-lived through its flowing rivers. With that life-force, I make you long-lived. Thus [he says] three times each, and "The triple life-force.
If he should desire, "May he live his full span of life," he should touch him with the Vātsapra hymn.
He leaves aside the last verse of this section beginning with "divaspari.
Having stationed five Brahmins in each of the directions, he should say, "Breathe after this one!
The one in the east should say, "Prāṇa! (out-breath).
"Vyāna," says the one on the right; "Apāna," says the one behind; "Udāna," says the one on the left.

He brings [the water] together; looking upwards, he should say at the fifth [step], or he should do it himself while walking around, if [others] are not available. He consecrates the place where he was born with the mantra: "O Earth, I know your heart, which rests in the moon in heaven. May I know that; may it know me. May we see for a hundred autumns, may we live for a hundred autumns, may we hear for a hundred autumns. (15–17)

Then he touches him, saying: "Become a stone, become an axe, become gold that is not melted; you are indeed the self named 'son,' so live for a hundred autumns. (18) Then he addresses his mother: "You are Iḍā, the daughter of Mitra and Varuṇa; you have given birth to a hero among heroes. May you be blessed with many heroes, you who have made us possessed of heroes. (19) Then, having washed her right breast, he gives it to him, saying: "This breast... (20)

With the two verses beginning "That breast of thine" (*yaste stanaḥ*), he places a vessel of water at the head [of the woman] with [the mantra]: "O Waters, be watchful among the gods; as you are watchful among the gods, so be watchful for this woman who has given birth to a son. (21–22)

Having established the *sūtikāgni* (the birth-fire) at the doorway, he throws into the fire, at the two junctions of day and night until the mother rises from her confinement, mustard seeds mixed with chaff, saying: "Śaṇḍa and Marka, Upavīra, Śauṇḍikeya, Ulūkhala, Malimluca, Droṇāsa, Cyavana—let them perish from here! Svāhā! Ālikhat, Animiṣa, Kiṃvadanta, Upaśruti, Haryakṣa, Kumbhīśatru, Pātrapāṇi, Nṛmaṇi, Hantrīmukha, Sarṣapāruṇa, Cyavana—let them perish from here! Svāhā! (23)

If the boy should be troubled, [the father], having covered him with a net or with his upper garment and having placed him on his lap, mutters: "Kūrkura, Sukūrkura, Kūrkura, the binder of children! Ce-ce, O dog, let go! Homage be to you! Sīsara, Lapeta, withdraw! That is the truth. Whatever boon the gods granted you, choose either that or the boy himself! Ce-ce, O dog, let go! Homage be to you! Sīsara, Lapeta, withdraw! That is the truth."
"If Saramā is your mother, Sīsara your father, and Śyāma and Śabala your brothers—if this is so, O dog, let go; homage be to you! Let Sīsara, the talker, bark in secret.
(24) He touches it; it does not bend, it does not cry, it does not rejoice, and it does not grow weary, [saying]: "Wherever we speak and wherever we touch. (25)
On the tenth day, having raised [the child] and fed the Brahmins, the father gives him a name:

(1) it should consist of two or four syllables, begin with a sonant, have a semivowel in the middle, end in a long vowel or a visarga, and be formed as a primary derivative (*kṛt*), not a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
(2) For a girl, the name should consist of an odd number of syllables, end in the vowel *ā*, and be formed as a secondary derivative.
"Śarma" for a Brāhmaṇa, "varma" for a Kṣatriya, and "gupta" for a Vaiśya.
In the fourth month, the ceremony of going out [of the house] takes place; he causes [the child] to look at the sun with the mantra, "That eye... (RV 7.66.16).

Having returned from his journey, he worships the house as before. Upon seeing his son, he mutters: "From limb by limb you are born; from the heart you arise. You are indeed the self named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns. (1) Then he smells the child’s head: "O Prajāpati, I smell you with the *hiṃkāra*; may you, [Name], live for a thousand lives and a hundred autumns. (2-3)

With the words, "By the *hiṃkāra* of the cows, [I place] thee," he mutters three times into his right ear: "O Maghavan, O Ṛjīṣin, grant us wealth that is all-encompassing and abundant, O Indra; bestow upon us a hundred autumns for life, and upon him, O Indra, O Śiprin, eternal heroes. (4) "O Indra, bestow upon us the most excellent riches, the insight of skill, and good fortune; prosperity of wealth, safety of bodies, mastery over speech, and auspiciousness of days"—with these words, he mutters into his left ear. (5)
But for a woman, he silently smells her head. 6. In the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) takes place.

Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* and offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), he offers oblations of clarified butter with the mantra: "The gods generated divine speech; animals of every form speak it. May that cow-like speech, lowing sweetly and yielding nourishment and strength, come to us well-praised, Svāhā! 2.

He offers the second oblation of the *sthālīpāka* with the verse, "May Vāja come to us," and with the formula: "Svāhā! May I enjoy food through the out-breath; Svāhā! May I enjoy fragrances through the in-breath; Svāhā! May I enjoy forms through the eye; Svāhā! May I enjoy glory through the ear. At the conclusion of the tasting, having drawn up all the flavors and all the food together into one place, he should then cause him to eat it.
According to the Śruti, the *hantakāra* consists of either remaining silent or saying "Hanta," for it is said that humans [are characterized by] the word "Hanta.

(6) For one desiring the expansion of speech, [the offering is made] with the flesh of a female *bhāradvāja* bird. (7) For one desiring food, [it is made] with the flesh of a *kapiñjala* partridge. (8)
With fish for one desiring speed; with the *kṛkaṣā* for one desiring long life;
with the *āṭī* for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).

For one who desires everything, [the rite] is with all [materials], or it is a sequence of food offerings; then follows the feeding of Brahmins, or a sequence of food offerings, then the feeding of Brahmins.
Prosperity! The tonsure ceremony for one year old.
Or on the third [lunar day] when it is unobstructed;
or the tonsure ceremony for a sixteen-year-old;
or for all [sons], according to custom.

Having fed the Brahmins, the mother takes the boy, bathes him, dresses him in two new garments, places him on her lap, and sits down behind the fire. While he holds onto her, she offers oblations of clarified butter; at the end of the consumption [of the remnants], she pours hot water into the cold water, saying: "O Vāyu, come with the hot water! O Aditi, shave the hair! "Shave the hair! (6) "Shave the hair! (6)
And [he performs the rite] at the hair-parting with the words "hair and beard.
Then he throws a lump of fresh butter, a lump of ghee, or curds there.
Having taken that, he shaves the hair on the right side of the head with the mantra: "May the divine waters, impelled by Savitṛ, moisten your body for long life and luster."
Having smoothed [the hair] with a porcupine quill, he places three young *kuśa* blades [underneath], saying, "O herb! (10).

Having taken up an iron razor, saying, "Thou art auspicious by name," he shaves it, saying, "I turn back [evil]" (11). With the verse, "With that razor wherewith Savitṛ, the knower, shaved the head of King Soma and Varuṇa, with that may the Brahmans shave this [hair] of his, for the sake of long life, so that he may reach old age" (11), having cut off the hair along with the roots, he throws it onto a ball of bull's dung held to the north (12).
In this same way, he does so a second time silently; 13. and for the other two [limbs], he applies sandalwood paste and so forth; 14. then, afterwards, [he recites] "Tryāyuṣam. 15.

Then, on the north side, [he says]: "By that path by which Bhūriścarā went to heaven and long beheld the sun from behind—that path do I shave for you with a sacred prayer (*brahman*), for the sake of life, for living, for great renown, and for well-being.
(16) Three times he moves the razor around the head clockwise, ending at the hairline near the face.
(17) "When the barber, with a well-fashioned razor, shaves and cuts the hair, may he cut the hair but not steal away the life of this person's head. (18)
Saying "The face," he touches the hairline with those waters; then, having sprinkled the head with water, he hands the razor to the barber, saying, "Shave without cutting.
The remaining hair is trimmed according to auspicious custom.
Having placed this well-concealed lump of cow-dung together with hair in a cow-pen, a pond, or near water, he gives a choice gift to the teacher;
at the *keśānta* ceremony, a cow.
There is a year-long period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) and shaving of the head at the *keśānta*; alternatively, twelve nights or six nights.
At least for three nights [one should observe the vow]. 24.
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age, or in the eighth year from conception; 1. a Rājanya at eleven years of age. 2.
A Vaiśya [should wait] for twelve years;
or, according to the auspicious custom, for all [castes].
He should feed Brāhmaṇas, and they bring him forward with his head shaven and adorned.
Having stationed him to the west of the fire, he makes him recite: "I have come to studentship (*brahmacarya*)," and "May I be a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*).
Then he causes him to put on a garment with [the verse]: "With that immortal garment which Bṛhaspati put around Indra, with that I clothe you for life, for long life, for strength, and for luster.

He ties the girdle [around her] with [the verse]: "This goddess, the fortunate girdle, has come to me, warding off ill-spoken words, purifying my pure color, bestowing strength upon out-breath and in-breath."

"Clad in a fresh garment and girt about, he has come; being born, he becomes even more excellent. The wise sages, seeking the gods with their minds and intent on sacred study, lead him forth"—thus [he recites], or [he may do so] silently.

"The sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) is the supreme purifier, that which was born from Prajāpati in the beginning; put on this foremost, auspicious, life-prolonging sacrificial thread—may it be strength and splendor for you! You are the sacrificial thread; with the sacrificial thread, I bind you for the sacrifice. Then he gives him the deerskin (*ajina*), saying: "The eye of Mitra, supporting, powerful, splendid, glorious, firm, kindled, unwearied, and ageless—this skin, O prize-winner, I put on. He then gives him the staff, saying: [the verse follows]. 11.
He receives it with the formula: "That staff of mine which fell from the sky onto the earth—that I take up again for long life, for sacred knowledge, and for spiritual luster.
(12) Some perform this like the initiation (*dīkṣā*), because of the statement: "He enters upon a long sacrificial session.
(13) Then he fills his joined palms with water from her [the bride's] joined palms with the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are most healing" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā*). (14)
Then he makes him look at the sun with the words, "That eye.

(15) Then he touches his heart while placing his own right hand upon it: "In my vow I place your heart; let your mind be in accordance with my mind; with one-pointed attention, enjoy my word; may Bṛhaspati join you to me. (16) Then, taking his right hand, he asks: "What is your name? (17)
"Here I am, sir," he replies.
Then he says to him: "Whose student (*brahmacārin*) are you?"

When he says, "Become [my pupil]," [the teacher replies]: "Agni is the teacher of Indra the student; I am your teacher; so-and-so is your [teacher]. (20) Then he entrusts him to the beings: "I entrust you to Prajāpati; I entrust you to the god Savitṛ; I entrust you to the waters and the plants; I entrust you to heaven and earth; I entrust you to the All-gods; I entrust you to all beings for your safety. (21) Having circumambulated the fire clockwise, he sits down. (1)

Having offered the oblations of clarified butter while being touched by the student, and at the conclusion of the consumption [of the remnants], he then instructs him: "O student, sip water; perform your duties; do not sleep during the day; restrain your speech; place fuel on the fire; sip water.
Then he recites the Sāvitrī verse to him—while he is seated to the north of the fire facing west, having approached and been looked upon by the teacher, who likewise looks at him.
Some say this should be done while the student stands to the south and the teacher is seated.
He should recite [the *Ṛgveda*] verse by half-verse, and the whole [hymn] together with the third [part], following it through repetition.
This may be done after a year, six months, twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, or three days;
or indeed immediately. One should recite the *Gāyatrī* for a Brāhmaṇa, because of the scriptural statement: "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed related to Agni."
The Triṣṭubh for a Rājanya;
the Jagatī for a Vaiśya.
Or for all [of them], the Gāyatrī [is recited] ten times; here follows the placing of the fuel-sticks.

With his hand he sweeps around the fire [with the mantra]: "O Agni, you who are well-renowned, make me well-renowned! As you, O Agni, are well-renowned and possessed of good renown, so make me well-renowned and possessed of good renown! As you, O Agni, are the guardian of the treasure of the sacrifice of the gods, so may I become the guardian of the treasure of the Veda among men. (2)

Having sprinkled water around the fire from left to right, while rising, he places a fuel-stick upon it with the mantra: "To Agni, the great Jātavedas, I have brought this fuel-stick. As you, O Agni, are kindled by the fuel-stick, so may I be kindled with long life, wisdom, splendor, offspring, cattle, and the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). May my teacher live long; may I be wise, not subject to rejection, glorious, radiant, endowed with the luster of sacred knowledge, an eater of food—*svāhā*!
(3) In the same way he offers a second, and likewise a third. (4) Or [he may offer them] with the verse "This for you... or as a combination of both. (5)
As before, [he performs] the sweeping around and the sprinkling with water.

Having warmed his hands, he wipes his face: "O Agni, you are the protector of the body; protect my body. O Agni, you are the giver of life; give me life. O Agni, you are the giver of splendor; give me splendor. O Agni, whatever is deficient in my body, fill that up for me.
May the god Savitṛ bestow wisdom upon me; may the goddess [Sarasvatī] bestow wisdom upon me.
"May Sarasvatī bestow wisdom; may the two divine Aśvins, adorned with lotus-garlands, bestow it," [he says].

(8) Touching his limbs, he mutters: "And may my limbs swell—speech, breath, sight, hearing, glory, and strength. He makes three marks with ashes on the forehead, the neck, the right shoulder, and the heart, reciting for each: "The triple life-span" (*tryāyuṣam*). (4)
In this regard, there is the practice of wandering for alms:
a Brāhmaṇa should beg with "bhavat" at the beginning;
a Rājanya, with "bhavat" in the middle.
From a woman of the Bhavadantī caste, a Vaiśya [is born];
there are three [wives] who are not to be rejected;
[the sons] are six, twelve, or unlimited in number.
Some say that the mother is the first [to whom the alms are offered].
Others say that, having presented the alms-food to the teacher, he should remain silent for the remainder of the day.
Having fetched firewood from the forest without causing injury [to living beings] and having placed it on that fire as before, he releases his speech.
He should sleep on the ground, abstain from alkaline substances and salt,
carry a staff, tend the sacred fire, serve his teacher, and subsist by begging for alms.
He should avoid honey, meat, bathing, sitting on high seats, sexual intercourse with women, falsehood, and taking what is not given.
One should practice the Vedic student-life (brahmacarya) for forty-eight years; or twelve years for each Veda;
or until [the texts] have been mastered.
The garments shall be made of hemp, linen, or wool; 16. for a Brāhmaṇa, an upper garment of black antelope skin; 17. for a Rājanya, one of Ruru-deer skin; 18.
For a Vaiśya, [the sacrificial cord] is made of goat or cow hair (19);
or for all [classes], it may be made of cow hair, because that is the primary material when others are unavailable (20);
the girdle of a Brāhmaṇa is made of Muñja grass (21).
The bowstring of a Kṣatriya is made of *maurvī* fiber (22);
that of a Vaiśya is made of *maurvī* fiber (23); in the absence of *muñja* grass, it may be made of *kuśa*, *aśmantaka*, or *balvaja* fibers (24).
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa is made of *pālāśa* wood (25); that of a Rājanya is made of *bailva* wood (26);
that of a Vaiśya is made of *audumbara* wood (27).
The beard of a Brāhmaṇa should be trimmed level with the hair; that of a Kṣatriya, level with the forehead; that of a Vaiśya, level with the nose; or all may be trimmed for all classes.

(28) When summoned by his teacher, he should rise and respond. (29) If the teacher is lying down, he should respond while sitting; if the teacher is sitting, while standing; if the teacher is standing, while approaching him; and if the teacher is approaching, while running after him. (30)
Behaving in this manner, he acquires the reputation of a *snātaka*: "He dwells there today; he dwells there today.

(31) There are three kinds of *snātakas*: the one who has bathed in knowledge (*vidyā-snātaka*), the one who has bathed in vows (*vrata-snātaka*), and the one who has bathed in both knowledge and vows (*vidyā-vrata-snātaka*).
(32) He who returns home after completing the Veda but before completing his vows is a *vidyā-snātaka*. (33)
He who returns home having completed his vows but not having completed the Veda is a *vratasnātaka* (34).
He who returns home having completed both is a *vidyāvratasnātaka* (35).
For a Brāhmaṇa, the time for returning does not expire until the sixteenth year (36).
Up to the twenty-second year for a Kṣatriya (37), and up to the twenty-fourth year for a Vaiśya (38); beyond this, they become those who have fallen from the Sāvitrī (39).

They shall not initiate them, nor teach them, nor officiate sacrifices for them, nor have any dealings with them. (40) If this lapse of time has occurred, they should be treated according to the fixed rule. (41) For those whose *sāvitrī* has been lost through three generations, there may be the sacramental rite for their offspring, but no teaching [of the Veda]. (42)

Desiring to perform the purificatory rites for them, one should sacrifice with the Vrātyastoma; then, according to the scriptural statement, "they may study as they wish and become eligible for social intercourse," one should bathe upon completing the Veda. 1.43.1.
1. Or, he may observe the life of celibacy for forty-eight years; 2. some say even for twelve years; 3. [he may do so] when permitted by his teacher.
The Veda consists of injunctions, that which is to be enjoined, and reasoning; some say it has six limbs; [it does not apply] to the ritual manual alone.
However, according to the ritualist’s preference:

having clasped the feet of the teacher and placed fuel-sticks upon the fire, standing to the east on *kuśa* grass with the tips pointing eastward to the north of the enclosed space, he takes water from one of eight water-pots with the mantra:

"The fires that have entered into the waters—Gohya, Upagohya, Mayūṣa, Manohā, Skhala, Viruja, Tanūdūṣi, and Indriyahā—I leave them behind; that which is radiant, that I take here. Thus he takes water from one [pot].
With that he sprinkles him. With this [verse]: "With that I sprinkle myself for prosperity, for glory, for sacred knowledge, and for the splendor of sacred knowledge" (11);
with this [verse]: "That whereby you two, O Aśvins, created prosperity, whereby you touched the *surā*, whereby you sprinkled the eyes—that glory of yours, O Aśvins" (12);
and with each verse of the hymn beginning "O Waters, you are most beneficent" (13).
With three [verses] he remains silent; with the others, having loosened his girdle with "ud uttamam," having set down his staff and put on another garment, he worships the sun.

"Rising, shining, and fierce, Indra has mounted with the Maruts who travel at dawn; you are the winner of ten, make me a winner of ten; find me, bring me hither. Rising, shining, and fierce, Indra has mounted with the Maruts who travel by day; you are the winner of a hundred, make me a winner of a hundred; find me, bring me hither. Rising, shining, and fierce, Indra has mounted with the Maruts who travel at evening; you are the winner of a thousand, make me a winner of a thousand; find me, bring me hither. (16)

Having consumed curd and sesame seeds, or having trimmed his matted hair, body hair, and nails, he should clean his teeth with a twig of the *udumbara* tree, reciting: "For the sake of food, arrange yourselves; King Soma has arrived. He shall wipe my mouth with glory and with fortune.
(17) Having rubbed himself down and bathed again, he applies ointment to his nostrils and his face, reciting: "Satisfy my out-breath and in-breath; satisfy my sight; satisfy my hearing. (18)

With the words, "O Fathers, be purified," he pours water for the washing of the hands from right to left; having anointed himself, he should mutter: "May I be well-eyed with my eyes, well-favored with my mouth, and may I be well-hearing with my ears. (19) He should put on a garment that is either new or washed, provided it has not been used for excrement: "I shall clothe myself for glory, for the granting of glory, for long life and reaching old age. May I live a hundred abundant autumns; I shall clothe myself for the increase of wealth. (20)
Then the upper garment: "May Heaven and Earth grant me glory; may Indra and Bṛhaspati grant me glory; may Bhaga find glory for me; may glory come to me.
(21) If there is only one [garment], he should cover it with the second half-verse.
(22) He receives the *sumanas* flowers with: "Those which Jamadagni brought for faith, for wisdom, for desire, and for sensory power—those I receive along with glory and fortune. (23)
Then he ties [the garland] on with the formula: "The great and wide glory that Indra has wrought for the Apsarases—with that, I tie these flowers together, consisting of glory.

(24) He wraps his head with a turban with the verse: "A youth, well-clothed... (RV 10.85.23). (25) He puts on two ear-rings with the formula: "You are an ornament; may there be further ornamentation. (26)
With the words, "Of Vṛtra," he anoints his two eyes (27).

With the words, "Thou art radiant," he looks at himself in a mirror (28). He takes up the parasol with the words, "Thou art the covering of Bṛhaspati; do not conceal me from evil; do not conceal me from splendor and glory" (29).
"May you two be firm; protect me from all sides," with these words he puts on his sandals.
"Protect me from all destructive powers on every side," with these words he takes up a bamboo staff.
He should always perform the cleansing of teeth and so forth, as well as [the wearing of] new clothing, an umbrella, and sandals.
If [it is] a mantra, [there are] thirty-two [units].
We shall now declare the restraints (yamas) for one who has bathed: 1.
Desire and so forth are other [than those]. 2.

One should neither perform nor attend dances, songs, or instrumental music; however, one may sing at will or take pleasure in song, for there is a scriptural authority to that effect. During safe travel at night, one should not go to another village, nor should one run.

One should not look into a well, climb a tree, fall from a fruit, crawl through a crevice, bathe naked, leap over uneven ground, speak like a parrot, gaze at the sun at dawn or twilight, or go about begging for alms. For it is stated in the Śruti: "One should not beg after having bathed; indeed, by bathing, one conquers the alms. (6) One should walk in the rain uncovered, thinking: "May this thunderbolt of mine drive away evil. (7) One should not look at one's own reflection in water. (8)

One should not mock a woman who has not yet grown hair, one who is barren, or a eunuch (9). One should call a pregnant woman "one who will give birth" (10). One should call a mongoose "one with its family" (11).
"Bhagālam" means a skull (12).
"Maṇidhanuḥ" means a rainbow (13).
One should not point out to another a cow suckling her calf (14).
One should not void urine or feces on ground that is not covered by a fertile layer of soil; standing, one should wipe the anus with a piece of wood that has fallen off naturally;
and one should not wear a discolored garment.
One who is firm in his vows should be a protector; he should guard himself from all sides like a friend to everyone while about to study the *Śukriya*.
For three nights, he should observe the vow. 18.1.18–19.1.1.

One should not eat meat, nor drink from vessels made of clay; one should avoid looking at women, Śūdras, corpses, black birds, and dogs, and should not converse with them; furthermore, one should not eat the food of a corpse, a Śūdra, or one who is in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka).

One should not void urine, excrement, or spit in the sun, nor should one shield oneself from the sun. One should perform the purposes requiring water with warm water. At night, one should eat after lighting a lamp.
Or rather, he should speak only the truth;
even if he is consecrated (*dīkṣita*), he may perform [exposure to] the heat and so forth, provided that the *pravargya* rite has been performed.

Now, therefore, follow the five great sacrifices (mahāyajña). Having sprinkled water around the food intended for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, one should offer oblations with the utterance of "svāhā" to Brahmā, Prajāpati, the domestic deities (gṛhyāḥ), Kaśyapa, and Anumati. To the spirits and the household deities, he should offer three oblations at the water-jar; [then] to Parjanya, to the waters, and to the earth.
To Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ at the two doorposts;
to Vāyu and the Quarters in each direction;
and in the center, three [offerings] to Brahmā, Antarikṣa, and Sūrya.
To all the gods and to all beings, to their north (7);
to Uṣas and to the Lord of Beings, further on (8);
"To the ancestors, svadhā! Adoration!"—thus to the south (9).
Having washed the vessel, he should pour out the water in the northwestern direction with the words, "O consumption, this is for thee.
Having drawn up the first portion and having offered water for washing to a Brāhmaṇa, he should give it to him with the words, "Behold, this is for thee.
Then the mendicants and guests should share the food according to their merit.
The householders, from the youngest to the eldest, should eat according to their rank (13).

Afterward, the householder and his wife [should eat] (14), or else the householder first; for there is a Vedic revelation stating: "Therefore, the householder should eat first, even before the guests, as one who has performed the sacrifice to Sviṣṭakṛt" (15).
Day by day one should offer the *svāhā* oblation; in the absence of food, one may do so with anything from a piece of wood down to a vessel of water for the gods, the ancestors, and men.
Now, therefore, follows the opening of the term for study (*adhyāyopākarma*).
When the herbs have appeared, on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa under the asterism Śravaṇā, or on the fifth day of Śrāvaṇa under the asterism Hasta,
having offered the two portions of clarified butter, he offers oblations of clarified butter with the verse from the Ṛgveda beginning, "To the Earth, to Agni."
"To the intermediate space, to Vāyu," in the Yajurveda;
"To the sky, to Sūrya," in the Sāmaveda; "To the quarters, to Candramas," in the Atharvaveda.
"To Brahman and to the meters"—this [formula] applies everywhere (8).
"To Prajāpati, to the gods, to the seers, to Faith, to Intelligence, to the Lord of the Assembly, and to Anumati"—this also (9).
This very same [formula] applies during the instruction and the release of the vow (10).
11. All should recite after [the Hotṛ] three times the verse, "I have approached Sadasaspati... while holding uncrushed grains.
12. Having offered [the oblations] one by one, they should each place three fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood—fresh, with their leaves, and smeared with ghee—while reciting the Sāvitrī verse. 13.

And the students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins) should eat unhusked grains (akṣatadhānā) without chewing them, according to the previous ritual rule, with the words "May they be auspicious to us"; they should consume curd with the verse "O Dadhikrāvan."
He should offer as many sesame seeds as he desires for the number of pupils with a ladle, using either the Sāvitrī verse or the section beginning with "śukrajyotiḥ.

(17) At the conclusion of the ritual consumption of food, having addressed those seated facing west with the syllable "Oṃ," he should recite the Sāvitrī three times and the beginnings of the chapters. (18) For the followers of the Ṛgveda, these are the faces of the seers. (19)
The *parvan*s of the Chandogas [are twenty], and the *sūkta*s of the Atharvaṇas [are twenty-one].

All recite together: "May there be forbearance; may there be forbearance; may there be forbearance; may this sacred knowledge (*brahman*) be full of vigor. May Indra know that by which we do not come to hate one another. (22)
They shall not study for three nights;
there shall be no cutting of hair or nails.
Some [hold that there is] no study before the formal dismissal [of students] (25). On the day of the new moon during a windstorm, there is a cessation of all study (1).

Furthermore, upon eating at a *śrāddha* feast, and during thunderbolts, lightning strikes, earthquakes, and other portents involving fire, as well as at the junctions of the seasons, there is no study for the duration of that time (2).
Upon seeing a cloud when there is none expected, upon seeing any form [of a corpse], for three nights or at the three junctions of the day;
having eaten with wet hands, in water, at night, at the two twilights, in a village containing a corpse, or in a village where a public proclamation is being made;
while running; and upon seeing one accused of a crime, an outcast, or a marvel, or at the rising of a celestial body—one should remain impure for that duration.

In the midst of mist, during the sound of musical instruments, at the cry of distress, at the edge of a village, in a cemetery, when there are sounds of dogs, donkeys, owls, or jackals, or when the Sāman is being chanted, one should not study at that time.
When a teacher has died, one should descend into water and abstain for ten nights.
In the case of a *sātānūnaptrin* or a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*), the period of abstention is three nights.
They should spend one night with one who is not a fellow-student;
having studied for five and a half months, they should conclude their studies,
or else for six and a half months.
Then they mutter this verse: "Both sages, that law of ours which has flown away—having released the bonds of friendship from our friend, we cast off all ties of companionship.
Having stayed together for three nights, they may go their separate ways.
On the Rohiṇī day of the month of Pauṣa, or on the middle Aṣṭakā, they should dismiss the term of study.

Having gone to the edge of the water, they should satiate with water the gods, the metres, the Vedas, the Ṛṣis, the ancient teachers, the Gandharvas, other teachers, the year together with its parts, the ancestors, their own teachers, and themselves. Having recited the Sāvitrī four times, they should say, "We have ceased."
Thus they should say. 3. The ritual of expiation (*kṣapaṇa*) and the proclamation (*pravacana*) are as before. 4.
On an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), the yoking of the plough is performed under the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, dedicated to Indra. 1.
Having worshipped Indra, Parjanya, the Aśvins, the Maruts, Udalākāśyapa, Svātikārī, Sītā, and Anumati with curd, rice grains, perfumes, and unbroken grains, he should feed the bull honey and ghee.
With the verse "They yoke the ploughs" (RV 10.101.3), he should yoke [the oxen].
With the verse "May the ploughshares be auspicious" (RV 4.57.8), he should plow or touch the plough.
Because of the instruction regarding new fire and because of the connection with the sowing,
they should plow that unplowed ground after having consecrated the fire.
They should sacrifice to the deities of the *sthālīpāka* as before, while sowing both rice and barley during the furrow-sacrifice (*sītāyajña*).
Then follows the feeding of Brahmins. 8.
Now, therefore, the Śravaṇā-rite:
on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa. 2.

Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (pot-offering), along with uncrushed grains (*akṣata*) and parched grains (*dhānā*), and having ground more of the parched grains, and having offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), he offers oblations of clarified butter: 3. "Drive away the white-footed one, both by the front and by the rear! These seven progeny of Varuṇa, together with all the kinsmen of the King—*svāhā*!
4. "Indeed, no serpent was seen by the white one in his conduct. Homage and *svāhā* to Śveta, the son of Vidarva!"

He offers from the *sthālīpāka* to Viṣṇu, to Śravaṇā, to the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, and to the rainy season. (6) He offers roasted grains (*dhānā*) with [the verse] "containing roasted grains" (*dhānāvantaṃ*). (7) He offers barley-meal (*saktu*) mixed with ghee to the serpents (*sarpa*). (8)

"Obeisance, Svāhā! To the lord of the serpents of the south-eastern quarter, the pale ones, and the earthly ones; obeisance, Svāhā! To the lord of the serpents of the white ones, the wind-related ones, and those of the intermediate space; obeisance, Svāhā! To the overcomer, the lord of the serpents of the solar ones and those of the sky.

(9) Having offered the entire cake on one potsherd with the formula, "Obeisance, Svāhā! To the fixed, earthly one," (10) at the end of the consumption [of the sacrificial food], he places a portion of the groats into a winnowing basket, goes outside the hall, smears a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and while a firebrand is being held up, having said, "Let no one come between [the fire and the serpents]," he remains silent and causes the serpents to drink water. (11)

"O Lord of the serpents of the fire-region, the pale ones, and those of the earth, wash yourself! O Lord of the serpents of the white ones, the wind-region, and those of the atmosphere, wash yourself! O Overcomer, Lord of the serpents of the sun-region and those of the sky, wash yourself! (12) Having washed [the hands] in this manner, he offers the oblation of groats to the serpents, striking the ladle [into the vessel] each time, saying: (13) "O Lord of the serpents of the fire-region, the pale ones, and those of the earth, this is your oblation! O Lord of the serpents of the white ones, the wind-region, and those of the atmosphere, this is your oblation! O Overcomer, Lord of the serpents of the sun-region and those of the sky, this is your oblation! (14)
Having sprinkled water as before, he scrapes with the *kaṅkata* combs, saying:

"O Lord of the serpents of the eastern, pale, and earthly regions, scrape! O Lord of the serpents of the white, windy, and atmospheric regions, scrape! O Overpowering Lord of the serpents of the solar and celestial regions, scrape!
(15–16). He then offers collyrium, ointment, and garlands, saying: "Anoint yourself! Smear yourself! Put on the garlands! (17).

Having poured the remains of the groats onto a bare patch of ground and having poured water from a water-vessel over them, he worships with the three verses beginning, "Homage be to the serpents" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.5.18).

For as long as he desires that the serpents should not approach, he should walk around the dwelling three times, sprinkling it continuously with a stream of water while reciting the two verses, "O white-footed one, strike away [the serpents]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.2.8.3).
Having washed and heated the ladle and the winnowing-basket, he hands them back.
At the doorway, they should sprinkle water with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā.

Having placed this remainder of the barley meal in a concealed spot, then, after each sunset until the Āgrahāyaṇī festival, having tended the fire, he should offer the barley meal as an oblation to the serpents, taking it up with a ladle. No one should pass between him and the offering while he is carrying it away.
Having washed the ladle used for sipping water, he sets it aside;
(24) they eat the grains of parched grain that are not stuck together; (25) then follows the feeding of the Brahmins. (26)
On the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada, there is a sacrifice to Indra.

Having cooked milk-rice for Indra and cakes, and having spread [the cakes] with cakes, and having offered the portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), he offers oblations of clarified butter to Indra, to Indrāṇī, to Ajā Ekapadī, to Ahibudhnya, and to the Prauṣṭhapadas.
At the end of the consumption [of the food], he offers an oblation (bali) to the Maruts, according to the scriptural statement: "The Maruts are eaters of what is not offered."
On *āśvattha* and *palāśa* [leaves], because of the scriptural statement: "The Maruts stood upon the *aśvattha*";
[one should offer] with each mantra beginning with "śukrajyotiḥ," and with the face turned away.
He recites mentally [the hymns],
for the Śruti says, "These are their names";
he mutters the verse beginning with "Indraṃ daivīḥ."
Then follows the feeding of Brahmins; on the full moon day of Āśvayuja, there are *pṛṣātaka* offerings.
Having cooked milk-rice for Indra and mixed it with curds, honey, and ghee, he offers it to Indra, to Indrāṇī, to the Aśvins, to the full moon of Āśvayuja, and to the autumn season.
At the conclusion of the partaking, he offers a mixture of curds and *pṛṣātaka* with his joined palms, saying: "May what is deficient in me be filled; may what is full not depart from me, svāhā!
His attendants look upon the mixture of curds, honey, and ghee while reciting the section beginning with "May Indra come hither."
Having reunited the calves with their mothers for that night and for the Āgrahāyaṇī full moon,
he then performs the feeding of Brāhmaṇas.
Now follows the Sītā-sacrifice: 1. Wherever one may perform a sacrifice of rice and barley, one should cook a *sthālīpāka* (pot-offering) consisting of those very grains.
2. One who sacrifices for a specific desire may also cook a *sthālīpāka* of either rice or barley even elsewhere. 3.
4. There is no doubt because it has been previously enjoined; 5. there is cessation because of impossibility;
6. [the sowing] is in a pure place to the east or north of the field, in ploughed soil, without obstructing the harvest.
Or [the rite may be performed] in a village, because there is no contradiction due to the employment of both [fire and domestic hearth].

Where he intends to cook [the oblation], having smeared [the ground], leveled it, and sprinkled it with water, and having established the fire, strewn it with *darbha* grass mixed with that [earth], and offered the two *ājyabhāga* portions, he offers the *ājya* oblations. 7–8.

I invoke here that Indra for whom the earth, the heavens, and the intermediate quarters are encompassed by the days; may his weapons be auspicious to us—*svāhā*. Whatever is desired by me in this rite, O slayer of Vṛtra, may all that be fulfilled for me while I live for a hundred autumns—*svāhā*. May prosperity, wealth, the earth, rain, preeminence, excellence, and fortune protect my offspring here—*svāhā*. In whose presence there occurs the success of both Vedic and worldly actions...

"I invoke Indrapatnī Sītā; may she be non-abandoning toward me in every rite, svāhā! I invoke in this rite the fertile earth, garlanded with threshing-floors, rich in horses, rich in cattle, and full of pleasantness, which unweariedly sustains all living beings; may she be firm and non-abandoning toward me, svāhā! (9) He offers the cooked mess of rice (*sthālīpāka*) to Sītā, Yajyā, Śamā, and Bhūti.
(10) According to some, the offering is accompanied by the mantra. (11)
There is a cessation [of the ritual] because of the Vedic text: "The offerings are made with the utterance of *svāhā*.

(12) From the remnants of the strewing, he offers an oblation to the guardians of the furrow (*sītā-goptṛ*), saying: "Those who sit in front, armed with good bows and carrying quivers—may they protect you from the front, vigilant and never-failing. I pay them homage; I offer this oblation to them.

(13) Then, to the south, he says: "The unblinking ones, clad in armor, sit there. May they protect you from the south, vigilant and never-failing. I pay them homage; I offer this oblation to them. (14)

Then, from behind: "May Ābhuv, Prabhuva, Bhūti, Bhūmi, Pārṣṇi, and Śunaṅkuri protect you from behind—vigilant and unfailing. I pay homage to them; I bring this offering to them. (15) Then, from the north: "The terrible ones, equal to the wind in speed—may they protect you in the field, the threshing floor, the house, and on the road—vigilant and unfailing. I pay homage to them; I bring this offering to them.
(16) From what remains of the clarified butter, other than that used for the preceding [offerings], he performs the bali-rite as before. (17)
And women should also offer worship, because it has been practiced [as tradition].
When the ritual is completed, one should feed the Brahmins; when the ritual is completed, one should feed the Brahmins.
Śrī. 1. The eating of the new [grain] for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).

Having cooked a fresh *sthālīpāka* and offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), he offers two oblations of clarified butter: "To him who possesses a hundred weapons, a hundred powers, a hundred aids, the overcomer of enemies; may Indra, who has kept us alive for a hundred autumns, lead us across all difficulties—Svāhā! The four paths leading to the gods which extend between heaven and earth—of these, may all the gods here bestow upon us that which brings freedom from decay and victory—Svāhā! 2.

Having offered oblations from the *sthālīpāka* to the deities of the *āgrayaṇa*, he offers to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the mantra: "O Agni, make this well-sacrificed offering reach its goal; O God, protect us in all battles. Pointing out the good path to us, come hither; come hither with light, and grant us unaging life, Svāhā! (3)

Then he eats [of it] with the verse: "May Agni eat first; for he knows how the oblation is. May he, who is seen by all people, make the plants auspicious for us. O gods, you have led us from ill to well-being; through you as our food, may we enjoy you. Enter us, O Food, as our friend; be gracious to our offspring and our bodies. Or he may do so with the *annapatīyā* verse. Then [he eats] of the barley: "This barley, mixed with honey, which they ploughed for the sake of the forest-dweller along the Sarasvatī—Indra, the lord of a hundred powers, was the master of the plough, and the Maruts were the ploughmen."
"O bounteous ones! (6). Then follows the feeding of Brahmins (7).
On the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Āgrahāyaṇī rite is performed (1).

Having cooked the *sthālīpāka* and offered oblations of clarified butter as at the *Śravaṇa* [rite], he offers another oblation: "The night which people greet with joy, like a cow approaching, she who is the consort of the year—may she be auspicious to us, Svāhā! We worship that night which is the image of the year; having bestowed upon us offspring and heroic vigor, may we attain long life, Svāhā! To the Saṃvatsara, the Parivatsara, the Idāvatsara, the Idvatsara, and the Vatsara, he offers great reverence."

"May we, long-lived and unslain, abide in the good favor of those worthy of sacrifice—*svāhā*! May summer, winter, and spring, the auspicious rains, and the fearless autumn be gracious to us. In the shelter and security of these seasons for a hundred autumns, may we dwell—*svāhā*.
(2) He offers the cooked rice-oblation (*sthālīpāka*) with the words: "To Soma, to Mṛgaśiras, to the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, and to the winter.

(3) At the end of the consumption [of the oblation], having placed the remains of the groats in a winnowing basket, [the ritual] proceeds from the departure [from the house] until the final sprinkling. (4)
"He says, 'The bali offering has been cast out at the end of the sweeping.

(5) Having spread a layer of straw behind the fire and having spread an unwashed garment, those who have bathed and are wearing unwashed garments descend [to the ground]. The husband is on the south side, the wife to his north, and the others according to their seniority to the north.

(6) Having seated the Brahman priest on the south side and having placed a water-pot, a branch of the *śamī* tree, a clod of earth from a furrow, and a stone on the north side, he mutters while looking at the fire: "This fire is the most heroic, this is the most blessed, this is the best winner of thousands; may it grant us great heroism and preeminence. (7)
Afterwards, he makes the añjali gesture facing eastward before the fire with the three verses beginning, "The divine boat. They ascend the straw mat;
he addresses the Brahman priest, saying, "O Brahman, let us descend."
Permitted by the Brahman priest, they descend [to the ground], [reciting]: "Long life, fame, strength, food, and offspring. (11) Having approached, they mutter:

"May winter be good for us, spring be good, and summer be well-disposed toward us. May the rains be auspicious for us; may the autumns be auspicious for us. (12) With the words, "O Earth, be pleasant to us," they lie down on their right sides with their heads to the east. (13)
"They rise up with long life and good life through the rain of Parjanya and the seven abodes of the earth.
Thus, a second time, they are permitted by the Brahman priest. They should sleep on the ground for four months, or as they wish.
After the Āgrahāyaṇī full moon, there are three Aṣṭakās:
dedicated to Indra, to the Viśvedevas, to Prajāpati, and to the Pitṛs;
these are performed with cakes, meat, and vegetables, respectively.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the first *aṣṭakā*, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* and offered the portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), he offers oblations of clarified butter: "Thirty sisters approach the appointed place, putting on a common garment; the wise ones, knowing the seasons, weave them out; radiant, they move around in the midst of the meter. Svāhā! The luminous goddess Night puts on the sky, fulfilling the ordinances of the Sun. The variously formed creatures, being born, look upon her in the lap of this mother. Svāhā!"

The Ekāṣṭakā, performing penance, gave birth to a child, the greatness Indra. By him the gods overcame the Dasyus; he became the slayer of the Asuras through his powers. Svāhā! "You have made me, who am not younger, your younger sister. "This is the truth," they say. Seek this out. May I be in his good favor just as you are. Do not apply another mind to another mind. Svāhā! The All-Knowing One has come into my good favor; he has reached a firm foundation and found a ford.

May I be in his good favor, just as you are; O noble ones, do not apply yourself to a false thought toward me, svāhā! Following the five dawns are the five milkings; the seasons follow the cow of five names. The five directions are fashioned by the fifteenfold [stoma], sharing one common summit above the world, svāhā! The first dawn is the embryo of Cosmic Order (ṛta); one bears the majesty of the waters. One moves among the appointed places of the sun; one belongs to the heat (gharma), and may Savitṛ restrain the other, svāhā!

She who first shone forth became a milch-cow for Yama; as such, full of milk, do thou yield us [milk] for each succeeding year—*svāhā*. The bright bull has come with the mist and the light; the multiform speckled one, whose rite is fire, seeking her common purpose through her skillful work, bearing both the aged and the ageless, has come hither—*svāhā*. This first wife of the seasons has arrived, the leader of days, the mother of creatures; though she is one, the Dawn has shone forth in many forms; being undecaying herself, thou causest all else to decay—*svāhā*. 5.

He offers from the *sthālīpāka*: "May the earth be peaceful, may the intermediate space be auspicious; may the sky grant us freedom from fear. May the quarters, the intermediate directions, and the sub-quarters grant us peace; may day and night provide us with long life that we may attain, Svāhā! May the waters and the rays protect us on all sides; may Dhātṛ and the ocean drive away evil. May the past and the future cut through [all obstacles] for me; may everything be mine. Protected by the *brahman*, may I be well-guarded, Svāhā!"
"May all the Ādityas, the Vasus, the gods, the Rudras, and the Maruts be our protectors. May Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin bestow upon me strength, progeny, immortality, and long life—svāhā!
(6) "To the Aṣṭakā, svāhā! (7) The middle [Aṣṭakā] is with a cow. (8)
He offers its omentum with the verse: "Carry the omentum, O Jātavedas, to the ancestors.
On the following day, at the Anvaṣṭakā rites, for all [the ancestors], he performs the offering from the left sides and thighs in an enclosed space, according to the ritual of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
For the female ancestors as well, he provides pouring of liquids into the pits with *surā* liquor, along with libations, collyrium, unguents, and garlands.
If he so desires, he may offer [the sacrifice] for his teacher and for his pupils who have no offspring. 12.
And in the middle of the rainy season, there is the fourth Śākāṣṭakā. 13.
Now, therefore, follows the ritual of the sacrificial post (śālākarma). 1.
On an auspicious day, he should have a hall constructed;
into its foundation pit he offers an oblation with the formula: "To the unshakable one, the earthly, svāhā! (3)

He raises the pillar: "I raise this, the navel of the world, the stream of wealth that furtheres riches. Right here I fix the firm house; let it stand in security, sprinkling ghee. Rich in horses, rich in cattle, rich in pleasant speech, rise up for great good fortune! Let the infant cry out to you; let the lowing milch-cows call to you. Let the young boy with the calf come to you along with the moving creatures. Let the jar of flowing liquor and the vessels of curds come near to you."

"O great one, the wife of Kṣema, well-robed, bestow upon us wealth, O fortunate one, and heroic strength; may our leaf be full of vigor, like that of a tree, rich in horses and cattle. May wealth fill us; may this prosperity clothe us. With these words, he enters four times. (4) Having kindled the fire within, having seated the Brahman priest to the south, and having placed a water-pot to the north, he cooks a *sthālīpāka* offering. Having stepped out and stood near the door, he addresses the Brahman priest: "O Brahman, let me enter. (5)
Permitted by Brahmā, he enters [the house], saying: "I take refuge in Ṛta; I take refuge in Śiva.

Having prepared the clarified butter (ājya) and offered two oblations of clarified butter with the mantra "iharatir," he offers the subsequent oblations: "O Vāstoṣpati, acknowledge us! Be easy of access and free from disease for us. What we entreat of you, accept that graciously. Be auspicious to our bipeds and auspicious to our quadrupeds, Svāhā! "O Vāstoṣpati, be our protector; O Indu, increase our household with cattle and horses. May we remain unaging in your friendship. Like a father his sons, accept us graciously. Be auspicious to our bipeds and auspicious to our quadrupeds, Svāhā!"

O Vāstoṣpati, may we be united with your auspicious, delightful, and path-finding assembly. Protect us in rest and in exertion; grant us wealth. Do you all protect us always with blessings, Svāhā! O Vāstoṣpati, the dispeller of disease, entering all forms, be a most gracious friend to us, Svāhā! (7)

He offers oblations from the *sthālīpāka*: "I invoke Agni, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and all the gods; Sarasvatī and Vājin. Grant me a dwelling, O you who possess strength! Svāhā! I seek refuge in all the serpent-deities, Himavat, Sudarśana, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and Īśāna together with the world-protectors. Grant me a dwelling, O you who possess strength! Svāhā! The forenoon and the afternoon, both together with midday."

"Pradoṣa, Arddharātra, and the goddess Vyuṣṭā Mahāpathā—I seek refuge in all these; grant me a dwelling for the horse, svāhā! The maker, the transformer, Viśvakarman, and the plants and trees—I seek refuge in all these; grant me a dwelling for the horse, svāhā! The ordainer, the disposer, and the lord of treasures together—I seek refuge in all these; grant me a dwelling for the horse, svāhā! This dwelling is pleasant and auspicious, granted by Brahmā and Prajāpati, and by all the deities, svāhā! (8)

At the conclusion of the consumption [of the food], having placed the ritual materials in a bronze vessel—namely, leaves of the *udumbara* and *palāśa* trees together with liquor, grass from a verdant meadow, cow dung, curds, honey, clarified butter, *kuśa* grass, and barley—he should sprinkle them upon the seats and places of worship.

9. At the eastern junction, he touches it, saying: "May Fortune (*Śrī*) and Glory (*Yaśas*) protect you at the eastern junction. 10. At the southern junction, he touches it, saying: "May the Sacrifice (*Yajña*) and the Ritual Fee (*Dakṣiṇā*) protect you at the southern junction."
He touches it at the western junction, saying: "May both food and the Brāhmaṇas protect you at the western junction.
(12) He touches it at the northern junction, saying: "May both strength (*ūrj*) and pleasant speech (*sūnṛtā*) protect you at the northern junction.

(13) Having gone out, he worships the quarters, saying: "May both the Knower (*ketā*) and the Good Knower (*suketā*) protect me from the east. Agni indeed is the Knower and Āditya is the Good Knower; I resort to them; let there be homage to them; may they two protect me from the east. (14)

Then, on the south: "May Gopāyamāna and Rakṣamāṇā guard me from the south. Day is indeed Gopāyamāna and Night is Rakṣamāṇā. "I take refuge in them; let there be homage to them. May they two guard me from the south. (15) Then, behind: "May Dīdivi and Jāgṛvi guard me from behind. Food is indeed Dīdivi and Breath is Jāgṛvi. "I take refuge in them; let there be homage to them. May they two guard me from behind. (16)

"Then, from the north, may Asvapna and Anavadrāṇa protect [us] from the north!"—the Moon is indeed Asvapna and Vāyu is Anavadrāṇa; "I take refuge in them; homage be to them! May they two protect me from the north. (17) He enters the completed house: "The pillar is Dharma, the lintel is Śrī, the two door-panels are Day and Night.
