These are the houses of Indra, wealthy and well-fortified; in them I take refuge, together with my offspring and cattle. Whatever belongs to me, I am invited [into this house], surrounded by all my kin and friends, well-sheltered. To you, O House..."
"May our houses have heroes who are unharmed on all sides.
(18) Then follows the feeding of Brāhmaṇas. (19) Now, therefore, follows the placing of the water-jar. (1)

In the northeastern direction, having dug a pit like a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and having strewn *kuśa* grass, he fixes a water-jar (*maṇika*) therein—along with unbroken rice grains, *ariṣṭaka* fruits, and other auspicious items—with the mantra: "Thou art the ocean" (*samudro 'si*). He pours water into it with the verse: "O wealthy waters, you indeed rule over wealth; you bear within yourselves auspicious wisdom and immortality. You are the mistresses of riches consisting of good offspring; may Sarasvatī bestow that vigor upon the one who praises her.
And he does so with the three verses beginning with "The waters are most beneficent" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā*).

Then follows the feeding of Brahmins. Now, therefore, follows the remedy for diseases of the head. Having washed his hands, he rubs his eyebrows, [saying]: "From the eyes, from the ears, from the hair-tufts, from the chin, and from the forehead, I pull out the consumption (yakṣman) of the head. If there is a splitting pain, [he says]: "O half-splitter, Virūpākṣa, Śvetapakṣa, Mahāyaśas, and Citrapakṣa, do not let your head afflict me! 3.
For he indeed becomes secure. 4.

[The rite for] one who has been sprinkled with *ūtūla*: while sleeping, having poured his own urine onto a living horn, he should walk around it three times, sprinkling it toward the left. "I release you from the mountain, from the mother, from the sister, and from both fathers and brothers, and from all friends. O *ūtūla*, you are sprinkled; where will you go, you who have been sprinkled? 2.
It leads to heaven, is beneficial for cattle, produces sons, brings wealth, confers fame, and bestows long life.
2 Having carried the *aupāsana* fire to the forest and having prepared the sacrificial enclosure, he should sacrifice a beast to Rudra. 3 It should be a castrated male. 4
Or [he may sacrifice] a cow;

having cooked the omentum, he offers the oblation from the cooking pot, the portions, the omentum to Rudra, the fat to the intermediate space, and the portions mixed with the oblation from the cooking pot to Agni, Rudra, Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Aśani, Bhava, Mahādeva, and Īśāna.
At the end, there is the offering to Vanaspati and the Sviṣṭakṛt.
9. The sprinkling with clarified butter around the fire.
10. At the conclusion of the sprinkling, they perform the joint sacrifices for the wives: to Indrāṇī, to Rudrāṇī, to Śarvāṇī, to Bhavānī, and to Agni Gṛhapati.

He offers blood on bunches of Palāśa leaves as an oblation to the armies of Rudra: "O Rudra, those armies of yours that are in the east—to them is this oblation; homage be to them! O Rudra, those armies of yours that are in the south—to them is this oblation; homage be to them! O Rudra, those armies of yours that are in the west—to them is this oblation; homage be to them! O Rudra, those armies of yours that are in the north—to them is this oblation; homage be to them! O Rudra, those armies of yours that are above—to them is this oblation; homage be to them! O Rudra, those armies of yours that are below—to them is this oblation; homage be to them! (11)
He throws the omentum, smeared with blood, into the fire or buries it deep; 12.
Having stationed the animal downwind, he worships it with the Rudra hymns, or with the first and last sections (anuvākas) thereof. 13.
They do not carry this animal into the village. 14.
By this very [explanation], the cow-sacrifice is explained, performed with milk-rice (pāyasa) and not devoid of purpose;
its sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is a cow of equal age. 16–17.
Now follows the rite of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*). It is explained by the sacrifice of a cow (*goyajña*).
It should be performed on the full moon day of Kārttika, or under the asterism Revatī in the month of Āśvayuja.

Having established a well-kindled fire in the midst of the cows and having prepared the clarified butter, he offers six oblations with one mantra for each: "May Iḍā come hither... (RV 1.162.22). Then he offers an oblation to Pūṣan with the mantra: "May Pūṣan follow our cows; may Pūṣan protect our horses; may Pūṣan win booty for us, svāhā! (RV 6.54.5).

Having recited the Rudra hymns, one should offer a bull that is either one-colored or two-colored, or one that covers its herd, or one that the herd follows; it should be red, endowed with all its limbs, the offspring of a cow that has a living calf and is full of milk, and it should be the most beautiful in form among the herd. Having adorned this bull, and having likewise adorned four leading heifers from the herd, they should release them with the verse: "I give you this young bull as a husband; sport with him, move about with your beloved. May we not be unfortunate through seven births; may we rejoice in the abundance of wealth and in nourishment. With this very verse, they should let them go.
He consecrates the nave with the remainder of the section beginning with "mayobhūḥ.
Having cooked milk-rice (pāyasa) in the milk of all [the cows], he should feed the Brāhmaṇas.
Some also perform the animal sacrifice.
The ritual procedure for that [offering] has been explained by means of the Śūlagava;
When a child under two years of age dies, there is impurity for the mother and father;
for others, however, there is purity [immediately],
or else impurity for one night or three nights.
They bury the body without cremating it.
(5) If [the burial] occurs during the period of birth-impurity, the impurity lasts until the rising [of the corpse], just like the birth-impurity itself.
(6) In this case, there is no water-libation rite. (7)
From the second year onwards, all [relatives] should follow the deceased from the cremation ground;
some say they should do so while singing the *Yamagāthā* and muttering the *Yamasūkta*.

If [the deceased] was initiated (*upeta*), [the rite] is the same as for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), beginning with the selection of the ground and ending with the going to the water's edge.
If he was consecrated with the sacred fires, they shall burn him with the *śālāgni*; otherwise, they shall burn him silently with the village fire.
They shall request water for one who was engaged in sexual intercourse, saying, "We shall perform the water-libation."
"Do not do so again," [he says] when the deceased has been dead for less than a hundred years (14); "Do so," [he says] in the other case (15).
All the kinsmen descend into the water as far as the seventh or the tenth person (16).
17. While living in the same village, they should remain affectionate toward one another for as long as their relationship lasts.
18. They should wear a single garment with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (prācīnāvīta).
19. With the ring finger of the left hand, they should wipe away [the remnants] while reciting: "Driving away evil, may he shine brightly."
Facing south, they immerse themselves; 20.
They pour water for the deceased once with their joined palms, saying, "O [Name], this water is for you. 21.
Once they have emerged and are seated in a clean place covered with grass, there they should address them [with the following verses]. 22.
Without looking back, they enter the village in a single file, with the youngest at the front.
(23) At the door of their dwelling, having bitten neem leaves and sipped water, and having touched fire, cow dung, white mustard seeds, oil, and a stone, they enter.
(24) For three nights they remain celibate, sleeping on the ground, performing no work and uttering no speech. (25)
Having purchased or obtained food, they should eat it during the day, excluding meat.
(26) Having offered a rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to the deceased, they should mention his name during the washing of the feet, the offering of the water, and the subsequent washing.
(27) On that night, they should place that [rice-ball] in an earthen vessel within a basin of milk and water, saying, "O deceased one, bathe here! (28)
Impurity due to a death lasts for three nights;
some say it lasts for ten nights. During this time, they shall not recite the Veda.
The obligatory rites should be discontinued, with the exception of those pertaining to the Vratas; some say they should be performed in the domestic fire;
others say that someone else should perform these.
Those who have touched a corpse shall not enter a village until the appearance of the stars;
if it is at night, until the appearance of the sun.
The rites of entry and so forth are the same as for others.
Impurity lasts for one fortnight or two;
the same applies to a teacher (ācārya),
and also to both maternal grandfathers.
For women, those who are unmarried (shall perform the rites) for one another;
for those who are married, others shall perform them; and they [the married] shall perform them for those [the unmarried].
If he has gone abroad, they should offer water from the time they hear of his death onwards and remain so for the remainder of the period;
if the period has elapsed, for one night or three nights.
Now, optional water-offerings are to be made for the officiating priest, the father-in-law, a friend, a relative, a maternal uncle, and a sister's son.
And for married women,
having fed an odd number of Brahmins on the eleventh day with meat,
some even slaughter a cow dedicated to the deceased (preta).

In the performance of the *piṇḍa* offerings, the first *piṇḍa* should belong to the deceased father, provided he has sons; the fourth [deceased] should be excluded. Some say that [the offerings] should be performed separately for one year. (50–52)

But the *nyāya* (the rule of logic) is not that it becomes a fourth *piṇḍa*, according to the Śruti. 53. Day after day, one should give food and a water-pot to this Brāhmaṇa. 54. Some also offer a *piṇḍa*. 55.
If it is an animal victim, having bathed it and led it around the fires by the front, he fixes a Palāśa branch [to its head].
He should perform the encircling with the girdle, the bringing forward, the tying to the post, and the sprinkling according to the ritual procedure, as well as whatever else [is prescribed].
Having offered two oblations for the animal victim, he offers five others silently.
One should sprinkle the omentum with clarified butter and designate the deity;
this same procedure applies during the dedication, the tethering, and the sprinkling, as well as for the *sthālīpāka* offering. Having offered the omentum, one cuts off the portions (*avadāna*).
He offers all three or five portions mixed with the *sthālīpāka* oblation (7).
An animal limb is the sacrificial fee (9).
One should sacrifice to whichever deity [is presiding] and offer a portion to that deity, saying to him: "Convey this man [to his goal]. 10.
Between two rivers, one may either have a boat made or not. 11.
Now, therefore, follows the penance for one who has broken the vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*).
On the new moon day, he immolates a donkey as a sacrificial animal at a crossroads;
he should worship Nirṛti with a *pākayajña*; the offering of the portions (*avadāna*) takes place in the waters.
The cooking of the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) takes place on the ground; he should put on that skin,
with its hair upwards, according to some teachers.
For one year he should go about begging for alms, proclaiming his own deed.

Then he offers another two oblations of clarified butter: "I am one who has spilled his seed through desire; I am one who has spilled his seed. To the one who desires desire, svāhā! I am one who has been deceived by desire; I am one who has been deceived. To the one who desires desire, svāhā!
Then he worships [the fire], saying: "May the Maruts sprinkle me; may Indra, may Bṛhaspati, and may this Agni sprinkle me with offspring and with wealth."
This indeed is the expiation.
Now, therefore, follows the entry into the assembly hall:
"He approaches the assembly hall, saying: 'O Aṅgiras-like assembly, you are named Nādi; you are named Tviṣi; homage be to you. 2.

Then Sabhā and Māsaṃmitī, both daughters of Prajāpati and endowed with consciousness, enter. "May he who does not know me stand near me; let that person be conscious for the sake of praising [me]," thus one should mutter upon approaching the assembly. Having approached the assembly, one should say: "I have come as the conqueror, the Virāj, not to be shouted down; I am the lord of this assembly, difficult to overcome by force."

If he thinks, "This man is angry," he addresses him with this mantra: "That form of yours which belongs to the forehead, belonging to *manyaḥ*, the destroyer of anger—may the wise gods who practice sacred study subdue it. I am the sky, and I am the earth; we two lead away your anger, as a she-mule conceives no offspring. (5) Then, if he thinks, "This man is malicious," he addresses him with this mantra: "I take that speech of yours from your mouth; I place it within my heart. From wherever that speech has been deposited, from there I take it back. What I say is the truth; let him who is lower than me suffer. (6)
This indeed is the method of subjugation.
Now, therefore, follows the mounting of the chariot.
Having given the command "Yoke [the horses]," and when it is announced "They are yoked," he approaches and touches the two wheels with the words, "She is Virāj."
"Thou art the Rathantara," [he says] for the right [pole]; "Thou art the Bṛhat," for the left;
"Thou art the Vāmadevya," for the shaft-socket.

He quickly touches his private parts with the mantra: "The two hooks and the two side-hooks on both sides of the chariot, which follow the darkness at the edge of the wind; O far-shooting, powerful-winged one, may these fires of ours carry us across and protect us.
(6) He drives the right-hand draft animal with the words: "Homage to the one who moves by thought!

(7) Without reaching the deities, he should descend [from the chariot]; having stepped toward the Brāhmaṇas, he descends in their presence, and having stepped toward the cows, he descends in the midst of the ancestors. (8)

Neither a woman nor a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) shall be the charioteer. If he has traveled for a muhūrta, he should mutter: "May there be rest here; may you find rest here. Some say: "May there be rest for us here."

If his chariot should be weak, he should mount it and recite: "O Aśvins, may this chariot of yours not be harmed in difficulty or on uneven ground. (12) If it should break down, he should touch a pillar or the earth and recite: "O Aśvins, may this chariot of yours not be harmed in difficulty or on uneven ground. (13) For him, there shall be no affliction and no injury. (14)
Having traveled the road and unyoked the chariot, one should cause fodder and water to be given; for it is stated in the Śruti: "This indeed is the release of the draft animal.

Having approached, he touches the elephant, saying: "Thou art the glory of the elephant; thou art the splendor of the elephant. Then he mounts it, saying: "By Indra’s thunderbolt I step upon thee; carry me safely across.
By this, the mounting of the horse is explained.

When about to mount a camel, he consecrates it with: "Thou art the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, thou hast Tvaṣṭṛ as thy deity; lead me safely across. (5) When about to mount a donkey, he consecrates it with: "Thou art a Śūdra, born of a Śūdra; thou art indeed Agni’s double-seeded one;
lead me safely across. (6) He consecrates a crossroads with: "Homage to Rudra who dwells on the paths; lead me safely across. (7)

When about to cross a river, he recites over it: "Homage to Rudra who dwells in the waters; may you carry me across in safety. (8) When about to board a boat, he recites over it: "The good boat. (9) When about to cross, he recites: "The good savior. (10)
He consecrates the forest with the mantra: "Homage to Rudra who dwells in the forest; may you lead me to well-being.

(11) He consecrates the mountain with the mantra: "Homage to Rudra who dwells on the mountain; may you lead me to well-being. (12) He consecrates the cremation ground with the mantra: "Homage to Rudra who dwells among the ancestors; may you lead me to well-being. (13)
He consecrates the cow-pen with the mantra: "O mind, may it be well for me; carry me across safely to Rudra, who dwells in the dung-clods.
(14) And wherever else [he goes], he should likewise say, "Homage to Rudra," for according to the Śruti, "Rudra indeed is all this.
(15) Having been brushed off by the fringe of his garment, he consecrates it with the mantra: "Thou art a brush, thou art not a thunderbolt; homage be to thee; do not harm me. (16)
He addresses the thundering cloud: "May the rains be auspicious for us; may the bolts be auspicious for us; may those which you release be auspicious for us, O slayer of Vṛtra.

(17) He addresses a cow lowing auspiciously: "Auspicious by name. (18) He addresses a bird crying out: "O golden-winged bird, messenger sent by the gods, envoy of Yama, homage be to you; what do you say to those who have done evil? (19)

He consecrates the auspicious tree [with the mantra]: "May the lightning not strike you; may the axe not strike you; may the wind not strike you; nor the staff sent by the king. May your sprouts grow forth; may it rain upon you in a windless place. May Agni not harm your root. May there be well-being for you, O Lord of the Forest; may there be well-being for me, O Lord of the Forest. (20)

If he should receive anything, he accepts it with the words, "May Heaven give you; may Earth accept you. Thus, for him who gives, that [gift] is not exhausted, and what has been accepted becomes even more abundant. Now, if he should receive boiled rice, having accepted it, he eats of it twice with the words, "May Heaven eat you; may Brahman eat you; may Brahman consume you.
(21) Now, if he should receive a stirred drink (*mantha*), having accepted it, he eats of it three times with the words, "May Heaven eat you; may Brahman eat you; may Brahman drink you. (22)

Now, therefore, after having studied [the Veda] again and again, there is this non-rejection: "May my eye be discerning; may my tongue be honeyed speech; may I hear much with my ears. Do not take away from me what I have heard. You are the proclamation of Brahman; you are the foundation of Brahman; you are the treasury of Brahman; you are gain; you are peace; you are non-rejection. Enter into me as the treasury of Brahman."

"By speech I cover you; by speech I cover you"—may the power of producing, forming, articulating, grasping, retaining, and uttering vowels (*svara*), gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*), chest-sounds (*aurasa*), dentals (*dantya*), and labials (*auṣṭhya*) reside within me. May my limbs, speech, breath, sight, hearing, glory, and strength flourish.
Whatever has been heard and studied by me, may that remain fixed in my mind—may it remain fixed! 23.
The Supplements (*pariśiṣṭāni*).

Now, therefore, we shall explain the consecration of ponds, wells, tanks, groves, and temples of the deities. For that purpose, during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, on an auspicious day, and when the lunar date, weekday, asterism, and astrological division (*karana*) are endowed with favorable qualities, one should cook a sacrificial porridge (*caru*) made of barley for Varuna. Having offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), he offers oblations of clarified butter with these ten verses: "Thou, O Agni, [be] ours... (*tvaṃ no agne*); "This my [prayer], O Varuna... (*imaṃ me varuṇa*); "For this reason, I implore thee... (*tat tvā yāmi*); "Those hundred [fetters] of thine... (*ye te śataṃ*); "And thou, O Agni... (*ayāścāgne*); "Up from the deepest [depth]... (*ud uttamam*); "Wide indeed is the king... (*uruṃ hi rājā*); "The support of Varuna... (*varuṇasyottambhanam*); "The face of Agni... (*agneranīkam*). Having thus offered these ten verses, [the ritual continues].

He offers oblations from the *sthālīpāka* with the mantras: "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Varuṇa! Svāhā to Yajña! Svāhā to Ugra! Svāhā to Bhīma! Svāhā to Śatakratu! Svāhā to Vyuṣṭi! Svāhā to Svarga! Then, as prescribed, having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, at the end of the ritual consumption, he throws aquatic creatures [into the water], adorns a cow, and causes her to cross [the water]. Reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*, he gives a choice boon to the teacher (*ācārya*), and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of earrings, garments, and a cow. Thereafter follows the feeding of the Brahmins.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rules for purification. Having gone far, having gone even farther, having placed the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) upon the head or the right ear, and having sat down with a blade of grass as a screen—facing north during the day and south at night, or facing north during both twilights—one should avoid the vicinity of fire, the presence of cows, and being in or near water; one should also avoid a mountain, the foot of a tree, a crossroads, a cow-pen, the presence of gods or Brahmins, a cremation ground, a place covered with ashes, and land ploughed by a plow.

One should void urine and feces. Then, having taken hold of the penis and risen, one should perform purification with water to remove all odor and residue. One should apply clay once to the penis, three times or ten times to the anus, and seven times to both hands. Clay should be applied once each to the hands and feet; this is the purification for householders. For students (*brahmacārin*), it is double; for forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), triple; and for ascetics (*yati*), quadruple.

Whatever purification is prescribed for the day, half of that is required at night; if on a road, half of that again; and if one is afflicted by illness, one should perform it according to one's ability.

Having washed his hands and feet, seated in a clean place, always with his topknot tied and wearing the sacred thread, facing either east or north and placing his hands between his knees, the twice-born should sip water from sources brought by non-Śūdras according to their respective order: reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate. They should not sip water with the lips apart, nor with fingers spread apart, nor while standing, nor while laughing, nor water mixed with foam or bubbles. One should drink three times using the *brahmatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to Brahman) and wipe the mouth twice.

In the right hand of a Brāhmaṇa there are five sacred fords (*tīrtha*): at the base of the thumb is the *brahmatīrtha*; at the base of the little finger is the *prajāpatitīrtha*; at the base of the middle of the index finger and the thumb is the *pitṛtīrtha*; at the tips of the fingers is the *devatīrtha*; and in the middle is the *agnitīrtha*. These are the sacred fords. 2.

When he drinks the first [sip], by that he gratifies the *Ṛgveda*; when he drinks the second, by that he gratifies the *Yajurveda*; when he drinks the third, by that he gratifies the *Sāmaveda*; if he drinks the fourth, by that he gratifies the *Atharvaveda*, the *Itihāsas*, and the *Purāṇas*. What flows from his fingers, by that all the *Nāgas*, *Yakṣas*, and *Kuberas*, as well as all the Vedas, are gratified. The rinsing of his feet, by that the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are gratified. When he touches his mouth, by that Agni is gratified; when he touches his nostrils, [by that Vāyu is gratified].

By touching the eyes, he gratifies Vāyu; by touching the ears, he gratifies Sūrya; by touching the quarters [of the head], he gratifies the Directions; by touching the navel, he gratifies Brahmā; by touching the heart, he gratifies the Supreme Self (Paramātman); by touching the head, he gratifies Rudra; by touching the arms, he gratifies Viṣṇu. [He should touch] the mouth with the middle and ring fingers, the nose with the index finger and thumb, and the two eyes with the middle finger and thumb.

"By touching the ear with the ring finger and thumb, the navel with the little finger and thumb, the heart with the hand, and the head with all the fingers—this Brāhmaṇa among embodied beings consists of all the gods," so it is said. Having thus performed the rite of purification, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā; one is glorified in the world of Brahmā—so said the Blessed Kātyāyana.
Thus ends the *Pariśiṣṭa-śauca-sūtra* composed by Kātyāyana.

Now, therefore, follows the daily bath (*nityasnāna*). Having brought earth, cow-dung, *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and flowers from a river or similar body of water, one should go to the water's edge and place them in a clean spot. Having washed his hands and feet, holding *kuśa* grass, with his topknot tied and wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Addressing the water with the mantra "Obeisance to Urvaśī," he should turn it around with the mantra "These hundred. Taking water in his joined palms with the mantra "May they be well-disposed," he should sprinkle it toward his enemy with the mantra "Ill-disposed. Then, having washed three times each with earth his waist, abdomen, thighs, shanks, feet, and hands, and having performed the ritual sipping of water again; *Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence regarding the washing procedure.*

Having paid homage, he should touch water and his limbs with earth while reciting "idaṃ viṣṇur" (RV 1.22.17). Facing the sun, he should submerge himself; having bathed with "udāpo asmān" (AV 1.6.4), he should emerge with "udidābhyaḥ" (TS 3.3.6.2). Having submerged and emerged again, and having sipped water, he should smear himself with cow-dung while reciting "mānastoke" (RV 1.114.8). Then he should sprinkle himself with water using the four verses beginning with "imamme varuṇa" (RV 1.24.14), and finally with "māpa uduttamaṃ muñcantv avabhṛtha" (AV 7.103.1). At the end of this, having submerged and emerged, and having sipped water, he should purify himself with *darbha* grass using the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" (RV 10.9.1) and "idamāpo haviṣmatīr devīr āpaḥ" (AV 1.6.4).

With two verses beginning with "apodevīḥ" and "drupadādiva," with the nine verses beginning with "śanno devīḥ," "apāṃ rasaṃ," and "apodevīḥ punantu mā," with the verse "citpatirmā," with the syllable *oṃ*, with the *vyāhṛtis*, and with the *gāyatrī*—both at the beginning and the end, while submerged within the water—one should repeat three times the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, or the triplet beginning with "drupadādiva" or "āyaṃ gauḥ," or breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) together with the *śiras* formula, or the syllable *oṃ*, or the remembrance of Viṣṇu. 1.

Having emerged from the water and put on two washed garments, having washed his hands and thighs, and having sipped water (ācamana), he should restrain his breath three times. Holding flowers mixed with water, with arms raised, looking toward the sun, he should worship him with the verses "ud vayam," "ud u tyam," "citram," "tat savitur vareṇyam," and the Gāyatrī according to his ability; and with the Anuvāka beginning with "vibhrāṭ," the Puruṣasūkta, the Śivasaṅkalpa, and the Maṇḍala Brāhmaṇa, he should perform the ritual salutation (upasthāna). Then, having circumambulated, bowed, and sat down upon Darbha grass with Darbha grass in hand, he should begin the Veda at its commencement and recite it according to his ability. 2.

Then he should offer libations, first to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Prajāpati, the gods, the meters, the Vedas, the ṛṣis, the ancient teachers, the Gandharvas, and other teachers; then to the year with its parts, the divine Apsarases, the Devanugas, the Nāgas, the oceans, the mountains, the rivers, human beings, Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, Piśācas, Suparṇas, spirits, animals, trees, herbs, and the fourfold host of living beings—saying "Oṃ" at the beginning. Then, wearing the sacred thread around his neck (nivītī), he offers to human beings.

[He should offer] Sanaka, Sanandana, and the third, Sanātana; Kapila, Āsuri, and likewise Voḍhu and Pañcaśikha. Then, [he should offer] to the south (apasavya), mixed with sesame seeds, to Kavyavāḍ-Anala, Soma, Yama, Aryaman, and the Agniṣvāttas; some also [to] the Somapas and Barhiṣads, and the Yamas. [He should offer] to Yama, Dharmarāja, Mṛtyu, Antaka, Vaivasvata, Kāla, Sarvabhūtakṣaya, Audumbara, Dadhna, Nīla, and Parameṣṭhin.

Saying, "Salutations indeed to Vṛkodara, to Citra, and to Citragupta," one should offer three handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds for each [deity]. Any sin committed throughout one's life perishes at that very moment. Even one whose father is living may offer these; others [should offer] while reciting "udīratām aṅgirasaḥ," "āyantu na ūrjam vahantī," "pitṛbhyo ye ceheha," and the triplet beginning with "madhu vātā. Having said "tṛpyadhvam" (be satisfied) three times and "namo vaḥ" (salutations to you), he should likewise [offer] for his maternal grandfathers, as well as for teachers, disciples, officiating priests, kinsmen, and relatives.

Having satiated [the ancestors], they drink blood from the body; having wrung out the garment and sipped water, one should worship with the mantras dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Sāvitrī, Mitra, and Varuṇa, using their respective characteristic marks. Having approached with the mantra "haṃsa," and having circumambulated, one should bow to the quarters and the deities. Sitting down, one should offer salutations everywhere with the words: "Obeisance to Brahmā, Agni, Pṛthivī, Oṣadhī, Vāk, Vācaspati, Viṣṇu, Mahat, the Waters, and Varuṇa, Lord of the Waters. One should wipe the mouth with the mantra "saṃvarcasā," and dismiss [the deities] with "devāgātuvidaḥ. This is the rule for bathing; this is the rule for bathing. 3.

Thus ends the *Trikaṇḍikāsūtra* spoken by the venerable Kātyāyana. The *Śrāddhasūtra*: One should perform the *śrāddha* during the latter half of the month, or after the fourth day; on whichever day it falls, one should invite the Brahmins either on that very day or on the preceding day. Some say [one should invite] *snātakas*, ascetics (*yatīs*), householders, or virtuous men, who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyas*), elderly, blameless, and established in their own duties. In their absence, even students may be invited, provided they are of good conduct. One must exclude those who are naked, those with white hair, those with discharging sores, those with black teeth, those whose genitals are pierced, the diseased, the deformed, the leucoderma-sick, those with leprosy, and those with deformed nails. When invited, one who is blameless should not depart from the invitation once he has been summoned. *Note: The text provided is a fragment of the *Kātyāyana-Śrāddhasūtra*. The translation reflects the specific content of this excerpt.*

Or he should not accept any other food; having bathed, purified himself, and sipped water, he should seat them facing east for the rite to the gods (*daiva*)—an even number according to his ability—and facing north for the rite to the ancestors (*pitrya*)—one or two for each, or three for the gods and one for the ancestors, or one for both, or the same procedure may apply to the maternal grandfathers as well, with the *vaiśvadeva* rite being performed as a single common offering (*tantra*).

Endowed with faith, one should perform the *śrāddha* even with mere vegetables; one should not let the latter fortnight pass by without performing it month after month, according to the Vedic revelation: "Your food [is offered] month by month. On that day, one should be pure, free from anger, unhurried, vigilant, and truthful in speech; one should avoid travel, sexual intercourse, fatigue, and Vedic study; and remaining restrained in speech, one should avoid touching [impure things], as should those who have been invited. 1.1.10–11.

The *śrāddha* preceded by the rite for the gods (*daiva*) has the same procedure as the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. For the rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*), however, the *darbha* grasses are doubled; he should offer [the oblations] with *darbha* blades in his hand while seated. In all inquiries, he asks the head of the row. Having spread *darbha* grass on all the seats, he asks, "Shall I invoke the Viśvedevas? Being permitted with the words, "Invoke them," he invokes them with the verse, "O Viśvedevas, come hither," scatters [rice], and mutters, "O Viśvedevas, hear this. He then asks, "Shall I invoke the ancestors? Being permitted with the words, "Invoke them,"...

Having invoked [the ancestors] with the verse "uśantas tvā," having scattered [the offerings] while reciting "āyantu naḥ," and having murmured [the mantra], he pours water into each of the sacrificial wooden cups (camasa) over which purifiers (pavitra) have been placed, using the verse "śanno devīḥ. Into each of these very same cups, he scatters sesame seeds with the formula: "Thou art sesame, whose deity is Soma; thou art the essence of the cow, created by the gods."

"May you, anciently mixed with waters and with *svadhā*, gratify the worlds of our ancestors, Svāhā!"—with these words, he gives [the water] into the hands of each [ancestor], which hold the *pavitra* grass, using one [ladle] for each, from whichever of the vessels made of gold, silver, udumbara wood, horn, or precious stones are available, or even from leaf-cups. [He recites: "Those divine waters which have come together with the milk, those which are of the intermediate space, and those which are of the earth..."

"May those waters, golden-hued, worthy of sacrifice, auspicious, pleasant, and easy to invoke, be favorable to us"—saying "This is the *argha* for such-and-such," he pours the remnants from the first vessel into [the other] vessels and places that vessel face down, saying, "Thou art the place for the ancestors. At this point, there is the offering of perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and garments.

Having taken up food smeared with ghee, he asks, "Shall I offer in the fire? Being permitted with the words, "Do so," he offers oblations as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. Having offered the remnants of the oblation and touched the vessel, he murmurs: "The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; in the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa, I offer nectar into nectar, Svāhā! With this verse addressed to Viṣṇu, or with a Yajus formula, he inserts his thumb into the food, scatters sesame seeds while reciting the mantra "Apo hatāḥ," and gives warm, well-prepared food according to his ability. While they are eating, he should mutter the Gāyatrī preceded by the Vyāhṛtis.

Having recited the *rākṣoghnī* verses, the mantras dedicated to the ancestors (*pitryamantra*), the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Apratiratha*, and other purificatory hymns—either once or three times, accompanied by the *praṇava*—and having ascertained that they are satiated, he scatters food, offers water once for each, and as before, mutters the *Gāyatrī*. He recites the *madhumatī* verses and the word "Honey, honey," and asks, "Are you satisfied? When permitted with the reply, "We are satisfied," he requests permission regarding the remaining food. Having gathered all the food into one place, he places three balls (*piṇḍas*) on *darbha* grass near the leavings after washing them, once the guests have sipped water; so says one tradition.

When they have sipped water, one should offer water, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and the water for inexhaustibility (akṣayyodaka). When it is said, "May the ancestors be free from harm," one should say, "May they be so. When it is said, "May our lineage increase," one should say, "May it increase; may our givers increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny."

Having accepted the blessings, "May faith not depart from us, and may there be much for us to give," he spreads out *kuśa* grass with its tips intact upon which the *svadhā*-invocation is to be performed. He asks, "Shall I cause the *svadhā* to be recited? Being permitted with the words, "Let it be recited," he says, "Let the *svadhā* be uttered for the fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers. When [the response] "Let there be *svadhā*" is uttered, he pours water onto the *svadhā*-invoking vessels. Then, having turned the vessel face upwards, he says, "Strength (*ūrj*)."

One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins according to one's ability, having caused them to recite for the *daiva* rite, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," and having dismissed them with the verse, "In every battle (*vāje-vāje vata*)," one should follow them with the mantra, "May we obtain strength (*amā vājasya*"), circumambulate them clockwise, and sit down. Now, regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa* (rite for a single deceased person): there is one *argha* offering, one purifier (*pavitra*), and one funeral cake (*piṇḍa*). There is no invocation (*āvāhana*), no offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and no Viśvedevas here. The question regarding satisfaction is, "Is it well-savored? (*svaditam*); the others should say, "It is well-savored" (*susvaditam*). In place of the formula for imperishability (*akṣayya-sthāna*), one says, "May [the deceased] be present" (*upatiṣṭhatām*). The dismissal is, "May you be delighted" (*abhiramyatām*); the others say, "We have been delighted" (*abhiratāḥ smaḥ*). 3–4.

Then, when a year has passed—whether at the end of three fortnights, on the twelfth day, or on whatever day an auspicious occasion (*vṛddhi*) may occur—he should fill four vessels with water scented with sesame and fragrant substances: three for the ancestors and one for the deceased (*preta*). He pours the vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the ancestors with the two verses beginning, "Those who are common... (*ye samānāḥ*). By this same procedure, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is explained. Thereafter, year after year, he should offer food to the deceased on the very day the deceased passed away.

In rites for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), the ritual service is performed clockwise; it is conducted in the forenoon, excluding the *pitrya* mantras, with the recitation of prayers, using straight *darbha* grass, and using barley in place of sesame seeds. The question regarding satisfaction is "Is it complete? (*saṃpannam*); the others should reply, "It is well completed" (*susaṃpannam*). The funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) are mixed with curd, jujube fruits, and unhusked rice. He asks, "Shall I invoke the *nāndīmukha* ancestors? Being permitted with the words "Invoke them," he says, "May the *nāndīmukha* ancestors be pleased. In place of the word "imperishable" (*akṣayya*), he asks, "Shall I cause the *nāndīmukha* ancestors to pronounce [the benediction]? Being permitted with the words "Let it be pronounced," [he says] "O *nāndīmukha* [ancestors]..."

"May the fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers be pleased"—with these words he should not utter *svadhā*; in this case, he should feed an even number of guests.

Now, satisfaction lasts for one month with cultivated herbs; in their absence, satisfaction lasts for two months with wild roots, fruits, herbs, or grain. They satisfy [the ancestors] further with these. Having sacrificed, purchased, or obtained goats, sheep, and rams—having brought them themselves, but not those that died naturally—one should cook them. For two months [they are satisfied] by fish; for three months by the meat of the *hariṇa* deer; for four by the meat of the ram (*aurabhra*); for five by the meat of birds (*śākuna*); for six by goat meat; for seven by tortoise meat; for eight by boar meat; for nine by mutton; for ten by buffalo meat; and for eleven months by the meat of the spotted deer (*pārṣata*).
For one year he should subsist on cow's milk or rice-porridge; for twelve years, on the meat of the vārdhrīṇasa antelope.

Now, regarding inexhaustible satisfaction: the meat of a rhinoceros, black pot-herbs (*kālaśāka*), iron-colored goat meat, honey, and large-scaled fish [offered] during the *maghā* asterism in the rainy season; and during the shadow of an elephant, those who study the *mantras* are purified. One who studies a single Vedic branch, one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, even one who knows only the essence of the *Gāyatrī*, one who maintains the five fires (*pañcāgni*), a *snātaka*, one who has thrice recited the *Nāciketa* fire-altar, one who knows the three *madhu* verses, one who knows the three *suparṇa* verses, a reciter of the *Droṇa*, the son of a woman married by the *brahma* rite, a master of speech, and a performer of sacrifices—these are to be employed. In their absence, one should employ at least one knower of the Veda at the head of the row, according to the scriptural statement: "He purifies the row up to the thousandth place."

Now follow the rites for specific desires (*kāmyāni*). On the first lunar day (*pratipad*), women who are ill-favored [are born]; on the second, the birth of daughters; on the third, small livestock; on the fourth, sons; on the fifth, success in gambling; on the sixth, agriculture; on the seventh, trade; on the eighth, one-hoofed animals; on the ninth, cattle; on the tenth, servants; on the eleventh, wealth and grain; on the twelfth, base metals, gold, and preeminence among kinsmen; on the thirteenth, young men die there; on the fourteenth, those killed by weapons; and on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), everything. "On the new moon day, everything"—so it is said. 1.
I bow to the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss; the bestower of all objects of desire, who bears half of Śivā’s body.

Now, therefore, following the Śrutis and Smṛtis, we shall explain the rules for eating. Having sipped water (ācamana), wearing an upper garment, and having applied marks of sandalwood paste (śrīkhaṇḍa) on his forehead, he should enter the dining hall, smear it with cow dung, and sit upon a prepared seat in a clean place. He should always face the east while eating, never facing the south, the west, or any intermediate direction.

If one desires prosperity, one should face west; if one desires truth, one should face north; if one desires fame, one should face south. Having moistened five parts—the hands, feet, and mouth—except for the mother while still living, one should draw a mandala with powdered *nīvāra* grain, cow-dung, ashes, or water. It should be quadrangular for a Brāhmaṇa, triangular for a Kṣatriya, circular for a Vaiśya, and merely sprinkled for a Śūdra. Just as Viṣṇu, whose weapon is the discus, protects the three worlds.

"May this mandala-ash protect all beings. Then, having placed the food served upon a vessel on the ground, he should praise the food with the verse "Pitu naḥ stoma" (RV 1.84.18), consecrate it with the mantras "Mā nas toke," "Namaḥ vaḥ kirikebhyaḥ," and "Namaḥ śambhavāya," and sprinkle it with water, saying "Satyaṃ tvārttena pariṣiñcāmi" in the morning, and "Ṛtaṃ tvā satyena pariṣiñcāmi" in the evening.

Having touched the food with the Yajus mantra, "Thou art splendor, thou art pure, thou art immortality," and having meditated upon himself as Agni with the thought, "I am Agni," he should offer the bali-offerings with each respective mantra, beginning with the Praṇava and ending with *svāhā* and *namaḥ*, [using the mantras]: "To Bhūpati, to Bhuvanapati, to the Lord of Beings; to Citra, to Citragupta, and to all beings, obeisance!"—and [reciting]: "Thou movest within all beings, in the secret cave, facing in every direction."

"You are Brahman, you are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ*-call, you are the *oṃ*-syllable, you are the supreme abode of Viṣṇu; you are the spreading of the nectar—*svāhā*. Contemplating this mantra of Viṣṇu, having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), meditating on the food as nectar, remaining silent and free from the fidgeting of the hands and so forth, he offers five oblations of the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*) into his mouth. 1.

"An offering to Prāṇa, svāhā! An offering to Apāna, svāhā! An offering to Vyāna, svāhā! An offering to Samāna, svāhā! An offering to Udāna, svāhā!"—this is the sequence that Yājñavalkya maintains; Śaunaka and Baudhāyana maintain "an offering to Udāna, svāhā" [as the final one]. This sequence taught by Yājñavalkya belongs to the Vājasaneyins. One should not touch [the lips] with the teeth while sipping water.

One should consume [the food] with the tongue using the thumb, forefinger, and middle finger for the first [offering]; the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger for the second; the thumb, ring finger, and little finger for the third; the little finger, index finger, and thumb for the fourth; and all the fingers together with the thumb for the fifth. Regarding these offerings, the commentators on Hārīta state that they are not to be taken with the tips of the thumb and ring finger, whereas Baudhāyana maintains that all of them are to be taken with all the fingers.

Having abandoned silence, one should eat first what is liquid in form, then solid in the middle, and finally liquid again; sweet first, salt and sour in the middle, and pungent, bitter, and so forth at the end. One should eat as comfortably as possible, and while eating, one should not touch the food with the left hand, nor touch the feet, the head, the bladder, or another's meal. Having thus eaten according to one's taste, one should take the remaining food and [recite]: "Those base ancestors who eat the remnants of what has been left over from my meal."

Having offered [the water] with the *pitṛ-tīrtha* while reciting, "May the food given by me stand as inexhaustible for them," he should drink half of the water held in his hand with the mantra, "Thou art the covering of nectar, svāhā," and cast the other half upon the ground. Then, having moved away from that spot, he should cleanse his mouth with gargles, tooth-sticks, and so forth, avoiding the use of the index finger. 2.

One should not eat while looking at one's wife, nor with one's wife, nor during the two twilights, nor at midday, nor at midnight; nor without the sacred thread, nor with wet hair, nor with wet clothes, nor with only a single garment, nor while lying down; nor from a copper vessel, nor from a broken one, nor—except for vessels made of silver, gold, conch-shell, crystal, or bell-metal—from a vessel of iron or earthenware; nor from one containing a crack, nor on the ground, nor on the hand; nor should one be an eater of everything, but should leave over some of the food to be eaten, except in cases of necessity.

Having properly sipped water after [eating] ghee, milk-rice, curd, flour-mash, meat, and honey, one should pour out the remainder from the hand onto the big toe of the right foot, saying: "May the Person, who is the size of a thumb and rests upon the thumb, the Lord and Master of the entire world, the consumer of all, be pleased. Then, with the words "The drinks are refreshing," one should touch the navel; and with the words "They are immortal," one should thereafter [worship] Agastya, Vainateya, Śani, and the Submarine Fire (Vaḍavānala).

For the sake of digesting food, one should remember the fifth [deity], Bhīma; having touched the belly, one should remember Śaryāti, Sukanyā, Cyavana, Śakra, and the two Aśvins. One should always remember them at the end of a meal, for it is said that "his sight does not fail. Having thus remembered, one should perform the purification of the mouth, saying: "Obeisance to the Blessed Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya;
obeisance to the Blessed Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya. 3. Now, the illustrious...

I bow to the twelve names of the Lord of Yogis; I praise Yājñavalkya, the best of sages, who is auspicious in nature, radiant, the embodiment of the Vedas, victorious, and possesses the luster of Hari and Hara. 1.
I salute the Lord of Sages, Yogānanda, the abode of bliss, who has conquered his senses, conquered his anger, and is ever devoted to meditation.
(2) That man who recites these twelve names at the three junctions of the day [attains the highest state].
By the grace of the Lord of Yogins, one shall become possessed of knowledge and wealth. 3
